500092.name: Crisil Ltd
500092.summary: Crisil earns money two ways. Indian borrowers pay it to rate their bonds and bank loans, and S&P Global (which owns most of Crisil) pays it to do analytical work for S&P's own ratings. Global investment banks, asset managers and Indian institutions pay for research, benchmarking data and outsourced analytics. The unusual part is the mix: the rating licence is what Indian investors recognise Crisil for, yet about 70% of revenue comes from research and analytics, much of it billed in dollars to banks outside India.

payers.who: Indian bond issuers and bank borrowers, plus S&P Global for Global Analytical Centre (GAC) work
payers.pays: An upfront rating fee, an annual surveillance fee for keeping each rating live, and cost-plus fees from S&P for delegated analytical work

payers.who: Global investment banks, asset and wealth managers (Coalition Greenwich, Crisil Integral IQ)
payers.pays: Annual subscriptions for benchmarking data, plus multi-year outsourced research, risk and analytics contracts

payers.who: Indian corporates, banks, governments and multilaterals (Crisil Intelligence)
payers.pays: Fees for industry research subscriptions, data, consulting and credit/risk solutions

outflows.gets: ₹1,943 cr in CY2025, about 53% of revenue
Cloud, data licences and in-house tool development (amount not split out)
Cash for bolt-ons such as PriceMetrix (Toronto, consolidated from 7 Nov 2025)

outflows.who: Shareholders (S&P Global is the majority owner)
outflows.gets: ₹61 per share in dividends for CY2025

streams.name: Ratings segment (Crisil Ratings + GAC)
streams.how: The issuer pays, not the investor. A company pays an initial fee to get a bond, loan or commercial-paper rating, then an annual surveillance fee each year the rating stays outstanding. GAC is billed to S&P Global at a fixed margin over cost.
streams.driver: New ratings (bond issuance, bank credit growth) × fee per rating + growing base of surveillance fees + S&P delegation

streams.name: Coalition Greenwich (CIB and wealth benchmarking)
streams.basis: Part of RAS, 70% of CY2025 revenue; split not disclosed
streams.how: Global banks subscribe each year to competitor benchmarking, client-feedback studies and revenue-pool analytics. Renewals cluster early in the calendar year. PriceMetrix adds wealth-management analytics.
streams.driver: Number of bank subscribers × products per client × annual price; depends on banks' discretionary spending

streams.name: Crisil Integral IQ (outsourced research and risk)
streams.basis: Part of RAS; split not disclosed
streams.how: Teams in India do research, model validation, risk and private-markets analytics for global banks and buy-side firms. Billing is mostly by dedicated full-time-equivalent (FTE) staff or by project.
streams.driver: Billable analysts × rate per FTE in USD; scope expansion at existing clients

streams.name: Crisil Intelligence (India research, data, consulting)
streams.basis: Part of RAS; split not disclosed
streams.how: Indian banks and companies buy industry-research subscriptions, data feeds, credit-risk tools and consulting projects, priced per subscription or per engagement.
streams.driver: Indian credit and capex cycle, bank risk-tool demand, government and infrastructure advisory

mechanics: Crisil reports on a calendar year: its financial year runs January to December, so 'CY2025' (= Crisil's FY2025) ended 31 December 2025, and the quarter to March 2026 is its Q1 2026. Comparisons with April–March peers such as ICRA are therefore offset by a quarter.

Ratings: when an Indian company or NBFC wants to issue a bond or take a large bank loan, regulation requires a rating from a SEBI-registered credit rating agency (CRA). The issuer signs a mandate, pays the initial fee and gets a rating. Every year after that it pays a surveillance fee to keep the rating live. This builds an annuity: each year's new ratings become next year's surveillance revenue, which management credited for much of the ~20% ratings growth in Q1 2026. Fees are linked to the size of the instrument but negotiated, and competition among CRAs limits price increases.

Global Analytical Centre (GAC): Crisil analysts in India do research and surveillance work delegated by S&P Global Ratings, billed at a transfer-pricing margin over cost. Management says that margin is similar to the ratings business. Revenue grows as S&P delegates more work, and the parent's needs set the pace.

Research, Analytics and Solutions (RAS), 70% of revenue: most of it is earned from large global banks and asset managers in US dollars, pounds and euros, while most of the cost is Indian salaries. Coalition Greenwich sells annual benchmarking subscriptions (renewals are seasonal; about USD 4.5 million of renewals were pulled into Q1 2026). Integral IQ runs multi-year outsourcing contracts billed per analyst. Crisil Intelligence sells research and consulting in India.

Cash and working capital: rating fees are generally collected upfront or on mandate, and subscriptions are invoiced annually in advance, so the business needs little capital. Outsourcing contracts are billed monthly or quarterly in arrears. Crisil has no meaningful capex beyond technology, and it pays out a large share of profit as quarterly dividends.

What scales and what doesn't: once a rating exists, surveillance is cheap to maintain, and data subscriptions are close to zero marginal cost. Outsourced analytics needs headcount roughly in line with revenue, so it scales more linearly. This is why the Ratings segment margin (44%) is about double RAS (22%).

500092.costs: Crisil is a people business: employee costs were ₹1,943 cr in CY2025, about 53% of revenue, and the rest is mostly technology, data, travel and premises. Capex is light, and growth needs hiring rather than plant. Operating leverage comes from two places. In ratings, the surveillance base keeps billing while analyst headcount grows more slowly, which is how the segment runs at ~44% margin. In RAS, subscription products such as Coalition Greenwich data get better margins as the client count grows, while FTE-based outsourcing stays more linear. Because RAS bills in foreign currency and pays salaries in rupees, a weaker rupee lifts margins: Q1 2026 included a ₹14.4 cr FX gain, versus a ₹5.2 cr loss a year earlier.
moat: SEBI CRA registration and decades of default-study history: Indian bond investors, banks (for Basel risk weights) and regulators accept only a handful of agencies, and Crisil leads in corporate bond ratings.
S&P Global parentage brings global methodology, GAC work that a standalone rival cannot win, and credibility with global bank clients.
Coalition Greenwich's benchmarking data rests on many banks contributing data. Each extra subscriber makes the dataset more valuable, which is hard to copy.
Long, sticky relationships with large global banks: outsourced risk and research teams sit inside clients' workflows, so switching costs are high.
Surveillance fees: once rated, an issuer keeps paying every year, which gives the ratings arm annuity-like revenue.

kpis.why: Bond ratings carry higher fees than loan ratings, and issuance drives new-rating revenue
Bank-loan ratings keep growing when borrowers switch from bonds to loans
70% of revenue; every point moves group profit by ~₹25–30 cr a year (est.)
Flattered by USD 4.5 mn renewal pull-forward and PriceMetrix; watch for normalisation
Shows whether surveillance and new ratings outrun a soft bond market

risks: Global bank discretionary spending: a downturn in investment banking budgets would hit Coalition Greenwich subscriptions and Integral IQ outsourcing.
Bond-market cyclicality: higher yields (10-year G-sec near 7%) push borrowers to bank loans, which earn lower rating fees, and slow new mandates.
Gen-AI could automate parts of research and analytics work that clients now pay per analyst for, putting pressure on FTE-based pricing.
Rupee appreciation against USD/GBP/EUR would compress RAS margins despite hedging.
Related-party dependence on S&P Global for GAC volumes and pricing, set on a cost-plus basis by the parent.

532375.name: Tips Music Ltd
532375.summary: Tips owns the copyright to a catalogue of 32,000+ Indian songs, mostly Bollywood hits from the 1990s and 2000s, and is paid every time those songs are streamed, watched, played in public or used in an ad. YouTube, Spotify, Amazon Music, Meta and other platforms pay about 70% of revenue; the rest comes from public-performance, brand and publishing licences. Since songs bought decades ago still earn about 85% of revenue, a ≈100-person company runs at roughly 65–70% EBITDA margins.

payers.who: Digital platforms: YouTube, audio streaming apps (Spotify, Amazon Music, Apple, etc.) and Meta
payers.pays: Share of ad revenue per view/stream plus licence fees; subscription income is 10–15% of digital

payers.who: Public-performance users, brands, broadcasters and publishers (via Sony Music Publishing)
payers.pays: Licences for playing music in venues and events, ad/film sync use, publishing royalties

outflows.who: Film producers (incl. related Tips Films) and artists
outflows.gets: Upfront fees for music rights to new films and non-film songs: ≈₹60 cr in FY26, ₹90–100 cr guided for FY27
Royalty costs ≈₹38 cr in FY26
Distribution share for delivering the catalogue to streaming platforms (terms not disclosed)
₹166 cr dividends in FY26 plus a ₹44 cr buyback in FY27

streams.name: Digital streaming and video
streams.how: Platforms pay per stream or view from ad revenue (about ₹0.05 per YouTube stream per management) and a share of subscription income, under multi-year licence agreements. Tips runs its own YouTube channel (158 million subscribers).
streams.driver: Streams/views × rate per stream; paid subscribers growing ~30–50% a year

streams.name: Non-digital licensing
streams.how: Public-performance licences (now sold online) for venues, events and businesses; synchronisation fees for ads, films and shows; publishing royalties collected globally through Sony Music Publishing; TV and radio.
streams.driver: Number of licences and brand deals; public-performance market growth

mechanics: Tips buys the music rights of a film before release (about 5–6 films a year) or makes non-film songs itself, paying a one-time fee to the producer. Under Indian law a sound recording is protected for 60 years, so a hit bought once earns for decades. Roughly a third of new content comes from outside producers, a third from related Tips Films and a third is made in-house.

Warner Music distributes the whole catalogue (30,000+ songs in 23 languages) to Indian and international streaming services and to Meta; management said revenue linked to the Warner partnership was about 25–30% of H1 FY27, and the deal renews in FY28. Sony Music Publishing handles the songwriting (publishing) side worldwide.

Each platform pays according to its deal: ad-supported video and free tiers pay a share of ad income per stream, while subscription services pay from subscription income. Deals are negotiated for several years at a time, so a renewal (such as the delayed YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels deal) can step revenue up or down. Growth in FY27 is mostly volume (more streams), not price.

The cost of new songs is expensed in full in the quarter the music is released, while the revenue arrives over many years. That makes quarterly margins jumpy (PAT fell 4% in Q1 FY27 on a 21% revenue rise) but annual margins stable. Management targets payback on new content in 4–5 years and keeps content spend at about 20–25% of revenue.

Catalogue songs can go viral again on Instagram or YouTube with no extra spending; in FY26 one catalogue track reached 3 billion views on Instagram. That is why about 85% of revenue comes from content acquired more than three years ago.

532375.costs: Tips has almost no fixed assets and about 100 staff. The main cost is buying new content (≈₹60 cr in FY26, ₹90–100 cr guided for FY27), plus royalties (≈₹38 cr), small marketing (≈₹6 cr ad spend in FY26) and employees. Because the catalogue costs nothing extra to stream again, every additional rupee from platforms falls mostly to profit; operating EBITDA margin was 70.5% in Q2 FY27 and management guides 65–70% for the year. The only real swing factor is content spend: management warned that bigger film deals could push it to 25–28% of revenue and hurt margins. Cash is returned through dividends and buybacks.
moat: A catalogue of 32,000+ songs across 24 languages, with Bollywood hits from the 1990s–2000s that cannot be recreated and are protected for 60 years.
Scale on YouTube (158 million subscribers) and long-standing licences with every major platform give bargaining power and reach.
Content that repeatedly goes viral again on short-video apps, earning without new spending.
Industry structure: a few labels (T-Series, Saregama, Sony, Zee, Tips) control most popular Indian music, so platforms must license from all of them.

Content cost inflation as labels and platforms compete for film music rights; management says the market is overvalued.
Warner distribution deal renews in FY28 and its terms matter for a large share of revenue.
Related-party dealings with Tips Films, a supplier of new content, with limited disclosure.
Management transition: the company is searching for a new CEO after its previous CEO left.

532741.name: Kamdhenu Ltd
532741.summary: Kamdhenu owns a TMT steel-bar brand but makes almost none of the steel sold under it. About 100 independent franchisee plants make bars to its specification and pay it a fixed royalty of roughly ₹435–470 for every tonne they sell, which in FY26 earned ₹175 cr against brand sales of about ₹23,000 cr. One own plant at Bhiwadi supplies most of the reported revenue but little of the profit, so the reported top line understates how asset-light the business is.

payers.who: Franchisee steel plants (≈50 TMT units + ≈50 pipe/structural/colour-sheet units)
payers.pays: Fixed royalty per tonne of Kamdhenu-branded product sold (avg ₹435/t in FY26)

payers.who: Distributors and dealers buying from the own Bhiwadi plant
payers.pays: Full price of TMT bars made in Kamdhenu's own ≈1.2 lakh t plant

outflows.gets: Bulk of own-plant cost; raw materials ₹142 cr in Q1 FY27 alone
Brand advertising that sustains the ₹1,500–6,000/t retail premium (amount not disclosed)
Quality audits and training of franchisee staff at Bhiwadi
Dividend ₹0.40/share for FY26; ≈₹300 cr cash, no debt

streams.name: Franchise royalty
streams.how: Franchisees pay a fixed rupee amount per tonne of branded product sold, not a % of price. Rates are reset at contract renewal; management aims for 10–15% increases a year.
streams.driver: Franchisee tonnes × royalty per tonne

streams.name: Own manufacturing (Bhiwadi plant)
streams.how: Kamdhenu makes and sells TMT bars itself through its distributor-dealer network. Revenue moves with steel prices, which are passed through; the plant also serves as R&D and training centre.
streams.driver: ≈1.2 lakh t at ~100% utilisation × TMT price

mechanics: A regional steel maker signs a franchise agreement with Kamdhenu. It gets the right to stamp and sell bars as 'Kamdhenu' within a designated territory, Kamdhenu's technology, design and quality specs, training for its staff, centralised advertising and access to Kamdhenu's 500+ distributors and 12,500+ dealers. The franchisee funds the plant, buys its own billets and raw material, and carries the inventory and credit risk.

For every tonne it sells under the brand, the franchisee pays Kamdhenu a fixed royalty. It was about ₹380/t a few years ago, ₹395/t at March 2024, ₹398/t in FY25 and ₹435/t in FY26; Q1 FY27 implies about ₹467/t (est., ₹48.1 cr on 10.3 lakh t). Because the fee is per tonne, a fall in steel prices does not reduce royalty income.

Why franchisees pay: management says the brand earns an average retail premium of about ₹2,600/t over unbranded bars (₹1,500–2,000/t in some states and up to ₹6,000/t in others), while the royalty is under ₹500/t. Brand access also helps franchisees raise bank funding. That gap is what lets Kamdhenu raise royalty rates at renewal.

Growth comes from two levers: more tonnes (FY26 franchisee volume +10% to 37.9 lakh t, against installed franchise capacity of about 52.5 lakh t a year) and a higher rate per tonne. Management guides about 10% volume growth plus 10–15% annual rate increases. New units are being added mainly in the South, which is only 13–15% of royalty and capacity today.

The own plant is a conventional steel business: it buys inputs, makes about 1.2 lakh t a year and sells at market prices. It provides about 77% of revenue, but management says the bottom line comes mainly from royalty. Its volume is capped because it already runs at full capacity.

532741.costs: Royalty income carries almost no direct cost: Kamdhenu does not fund franchisee plants, raw material or inventory. The costs that support it are largely fixed: brand advertising, the quality and field teams, and corporate overhead. So each extra tonne or rupee of rate increase falls almost entirely to profit, which is why FY26 PBT grew 31% on 2% revenue growth. The own plant is the opposite: a raw-material-heavy, low-margin business with steel price pass-through; Q1 FY27 gross margin was 33.4% for the company overall. Capex is small (a 5 MWp captive solar plant in June 2026 is expected to save ₹4–5 cr a year), and the company is debt-free.
moat: A long-established consumer-facing TMT brand with an estimated ~20% share of retail branded TMT, backed by national TV and celebrity advertising that a single regional mill cannot afford alone.
A 12,500+ dealer and 500+ distributor network that franchisees plug into; replicating that reach takes years.
Territorial exclusivity gives each franchisee protected regional sales, which makes the network sticky for good operators.
Low royalty relative to the brand premium (under ₹500/t vs ≈₹2,600/t) leaves franchisees clearly better off staying.

kpis.why: First half of the royalty equation
Pricing power of the brand; guided +10–15% a year
Near-pure profit stream; Q2 growth slowed from 15.6% in Q1
Shows how much royalty growth reaches profit

kpis.latest: ≈72% (FY26 est.: 37.9 lakh t on ≈52.5 lakh t)
kpis.why: Headroom for volume growth without new units

financials.note: Royalty ₹175 cr (22.9% of revenue); ROCE 26.8%, ROE 19.8%; debt-free

risks: Franchisee concentration and churn: 4–5 units exited and 4–5 joined in FY26; losing large franchisees in a region cuts royalty directly.
Brand damage from a single franchisee's quality lapse, since Kamdhenu does not make most of the steel sold under its name.
Pushing royalty up 10–15% a year may meet resistance if the brand premium narrows against Tata Tiscon, JSW/Jindal and strong regional brands.
Cyclical construction demand and raw-material/fuel cost spikes squeeze franchisee margins and volumes.
Use of ≈₹300 cr cash is still undecided; poor capital allocation would dilute high returns.

532835.name: ICRA Ltd
532835.summary: ICRA is India's Moody's-controlled credit rating agency. Companies, banks and NBFCs pay it to rate their loans, bonds and securitisation deals, and keep paying every year the rating stays live. Its other half, Risk & Analytics, earns fees from Moody's for outsourced analyst teams and sells risk and regulatory-reporting software to banks. That second half is now close to half of revenue but runs at a much lower margin.

payers.who: Indian borrowers: corporates, NBFCs, banks, securitisation originators
payers.pays: An initial rating fee plus an annual surveillance fee for each outstanding rating on a bank loan, bond, commercial paper or structured deal

payers.who: Moody's group (parent)
payers.pays: Mostly recurring fees for dedicated offshore analyst and data teams (KnowTech); ≈49% of KnowTech, so ≈14% of group (est.)

payers.who: Banks, insurers, asset managers and other R&A clients in India and abroad
payers.pays: Software licences, subscriptions and implementation fees (Fintellix, D2K), market data and valuation services, and non-Moody's knowledge services

outflows.gets: The largest cost line; drives most of the operating cost base
Unified product engineering across KnowTech, BankTech and CapTech
₹249 cr for 98.75% of Fintellix (Oct 2025) and buy-out of D2K to 100%
₹105 per share for FY26, including a ₹35 special dividend (~₹101 cr)

streams.name: Ratings and ancillary services
streams.basis: Q1 FY27 segment revenue (₹83.8 cr of ~₹164 cr)
streams.how: The issuer pays: an upfront fee to rate a bank facility, bond, CP or securitised pool, then an annual surveillance fee while it is outstanding. Agreements include a clause that lets ICRA reprice surveillance fees, and it has started using it.
streams.driver: Bank credit growth + bond/CP issuance + securitisation volumes × fee per rating; growing surveillance base

streams.name: KnowTech (knowledge services)
streams.how: Offshore teams do research, data and analytics work, mainly for Moody's. Billing is 80–90% recurring by FTE with about a year of budget visibility, and the rest is projects.
streams.driver: Moody's headcount budget and in-sourcing decisions; automation reduces FTE demand

streams.name: BankTech and CapTech (risk, regtech, market data)
streams.how: Banks buy Fintellix regulatory-reporting and D2K risk software: historically a one-time licence plus annual maintenance, now moving to subscriptions. CapTech sells market data, bond valuation and investment intelligence. Deals range from ₹10–20 lakh to multi-crore.
streams.driver: Bank regtech mandates (ECL from Apr 2027, Basel reset), new logos, annual renewals concentrated in Q1

mechanics: Ratings is the core. Indian regulation pushes borrowers to get rated: banks use external ratings to set Basel capital risk weights on corporate loans, and SEBI requires ratings on listed bonds and CP. A company signs a mandate with ICRA, pays an initial fee, and ICRA's committee assigns a rating. Each year the issuer pays a surveillance fee to keep the rating live. A large base of outstanding ratings means much of each year's revenue is already locked in.

Pricing is linked to the size of the rated instrument but is negotiated and competitive, as several SEBI-registered agencies chase the same issuers. Bond ratings earn more than bank-loan ratings, so the bond-to-loan shift (H1 FY27: bank credit +21.4%, bond issuance +3.7%) dilutes realisation. Management is now using contractual clauses to raise surveillance fees, after a competitor did the same.

Fees are usually collected around the mandate and the annual surveillance date, so ratings needs almost no working capital. Most of the ~37.6% operating margin comes from spreading analyst costs over a growing surveillance book.

Risk & Analytics began as captive work for Moody's. Analysts in India produce data and research for the parent and are billed mostly per head on annual budgets. Moody's is now about 49% of KnowTech, down from 80% five years ago, as ICRA has added outside clients. Growth has stalled because of automation and periodic in-sourcing, and the non-ratings run-rate has held near ₹80 cr a quarter.

To diversify, ICRA bought Fintellix (₹249 cr, consolidated from Oct 2025; ₹51.7 cr revenue and ~26% EBITDA margin in its first six months) and took D2K to 100%. These product businesses sell software to banks with upfront licence and implementation revenue plus recurring maintenance, and are moving to subscriptions. They need sales and engineering investment, and D2K and Fintellix together were still loss-making at PAT level in FY26.

About USD 18 mn of FY26 revenue (roughly a third) is in dollars, mostly from Moody's, while costs are in rupees. Group cash exceeds ₹700 cr, and FY27 cash generation of ₹180–200 cr was cited, which funds dividends and M&A.

532835.costs: Costs are mostly people: rating analysts and committees, KnowTech analysts billed to clients, and engineers and sales staff for software. Ratings has strong operating leverage, because the surveillance book grows each year without a matching rise in headcount, and margin has risen from 20.8% to 37.6% in five years. KnowTech cost grows roughly with billed headcount. BankTech/CapTech needs upfront product, sales and implementation spend, plus amortisation of acquired intangibles, so it earns lower margins until scale is reached. Capex is modest and mostly technology and AI tooling. FY26 PBT before exceptional items was ₹257.4 cr on ₹599.5 cr revenue, a ratio boosted by sizeable treasury other income on the >₹700 cr cash pile.
moat: SEBI and RBI accreditation: bank capital rules and bond regulations accept ratings only from a small set of registered agencies, and building a default track record takes decades.
Moody's affiliation (~52% owner) lends methodology and credibility with investors, and gives a captive, recurring KnowTech anchor client.
Surveillance annuity: rated issuers rarely switch agencies mid-life of an instrument, which gives a predictable base of fees.
Embedded bank software: once Fintellix regulatory-reporting software is built into a bank's systems, replacing it is costly and risky.

risks: Issuer-pays conflict and regulatory action: SEBI penalties or rating failures can damage the franchise and invite tighter fee rules.
Fee pressure from competition among Indian CRAs, worsened by the shift from higher-fee bond ratings to bank-loan ratings.
Concentration on Moody's for KnowTech: in-sourcing or automation by the parent cuts revenue directly, and the parent also works with other Indian providers.
Execution risk in software M&A: D2K and Fintellix are loss-making with no guided breakeven, and acquisition intangibles add amortisation.
RBI's Basel risk-weight reset (Apr 2027) could shift demand for bank-loan ratings in either direction; ICRA expects a positive effect but has not quantified it.

534091.name: Multi Commodity Exchange of India Ltd
534091.summary: MCX is India's near-monopoly commodity derivatives exchange: every time a trader buys or sells a gold, silver, crude or natural-gas future or option, the broker collects a small exchange fee and passes it to MCX. About 91% of revenue is these per-trade fees, so income tracks trading activity (and commodity price volatility) almost one-for-one, while costs are largely fixed, which gives 70%+ EBITDA margins.

payers.who: Traders and hedgers (retail, prop desks, jewellers, refiners, FPIs) via ~580 member brokers

streams.name: Options transaction fees
streams.how: ₹41.80 per ₹1 lakh of option premium traded since 1 Oct 2024, a single uniform slab charged to the member. Mostly gold, silver, crude and natural gas options; FY26 options fees ₹1,398 cr.

streams.how: ₹2.10 per ₹1 lakh of futures turnover (notional value). FY26 futures fees ₹693 cr; Q4 FY26 futures turnover was 77% bullion.

streams.name: Other operating revenue
streams.how: Membership and connectivity fees, terminal and data charges, and interest on margin money placed with the clearing corporation (₹59 cr in Q4 FY26). Company does not split this further.
streams.driver: Member count, open interest/margins held, data licensing

mechanics: A client places a trade through a broker that is a member of MCX. The order is matched on MCX's electronic platform and cleared and guaranteed by its wholly owned subsidiary MCX Clearing Corporation (MCXCCL), which collects margin from both sides so that a default by one trader does not hit the other. The broker adds MCX's transaction fee to the client's contract note and pays it to the exchange; MCX never deals with the end client directly and carries no credit risk on the fee.

Pricing is set by MCX, not negotiated per client. Since SEBI's 'true-to-label' circular of October 2024, exchanges must charge every member the same flat rate, so MCX replaced volume-based discount slabs with ₹2.10 per lakh of futures turnover and ₹41.80 per lakh of option premium. Management says there has been no fee increase since; growth is volume-led.

Options now earn about two-thirds of fees. Because options are charged on premium, not notional value, revenue depends on volatility: in Q1 FY27 bullion options premium fell 27% QoQ while notional volume rose ~116%, as the premium-to-notional ratio dropped from 1.03% to 0.35%. A quiet market can therefore lower revenue even when headline 'ADT' (average daily turnover, mostly notional options) rises.

Volume comes from two engines that alternate: bullion (gold, silver, including small 'micro' and 100-gram contracts that suit retail) and energy (crude, natural gas, electricity). FY26 bullion F&O turnover rose ~5x and energy 29%. Commodity price spikes, new contract sizes, far-dated expiries, and more retail participation via discount brokers (20.9 lakh traded clients in FY26) all lift turnover.

Cash arrives daily via member settlement, so working capital is negative and the business throws off cash. The exchange's cost base is mostly fixed (technology, people, licences), so the incremental rupee of fee income falls largely to profit: FY26 revenue doubled to ₹2,302 cr while EBITDA rose 133% to ₹1,774 cr.

Some costs do scale with volume: product licence fees for crude and natural gas reference prices (from CME) and SGF contributions linked to clearing risk. In Aug 2026 SEBI cut the stress-test requirement, so SGF contributions are paused for 2–3 quarters, flattering H1 FY27 profit.

534816.name: Indus Towers Ltd
534816.summary: Indus Towers owns about 2.7 lakh mobile towers in India and rents space on them to the telecom operators (Airtel, Vodafone Idea and Jio), who sign 10-year-plus contracts. It earns a monthly rent for every operator on a tower, so adding a second or third tenant to an already-built tower is almost pure profit. It also buys the electricity and diesel that runs each site and bills the operators for it, which makes up about a third of revenue but earns no margin.

payers.who: Mobile operators: Bharti Airtel (largest tenant and ~50% owner), Vodafone Idea, Reliance Jio
payers.pays: Monthly rent (called 'sharing revenue') per operator per tower, with annual escalation of about 2.5%

payers.who: The same operators
payers.pays: Reimbursement of grid power and diesel used to run their equipment at each site (energy pass-through)

Ground and rooftop site rent (shown as lease depreciation ₹2,713 cr and lease interest ₹1,600 cr in FY26)

outflows.gets: Capex of ₹8,817 cr in FY26 for new towers, 5G upgrades, batteries and solar
Repairs and maintenance ₹1,467 cr and employee costs ₹878 cr in FY26

streams.name: Tower sharing (rental) revenue
streams.how: Each operator on a tower pays a monthly rent under a master service agreement (MSA); the rent covers the steel structure, site, security and maintenance, and rises with a contractual escalator (about 2.5% a year). New contracts and renewals run at least 10 years.
streams.driver: Towers × tenants per tower (sharing factor 1.62–1.63) × rent per tenant

streams.name: Energy reimbursements
streams.how: Indus pays the electricity board and buys diesel for back-up generators, then bills operators based on agreed consumption norms or actual diesel prices. It is a pass-through, and in practice runs at a small loss (energy margin −3.6% in Q2 FY27).
streams.driver: Sites × power load per tenant × grid tariff and diesel price

streams.name: Equipment sales and other
streams.how: Small sales of goods and related services (₹15.6 cr in FY26). In-building (IBS) and DAS solutions for metros, tunnels and malls are growing but described as very small.
streams.driver: Project wins

mechanics: An operator wanting coverage in an area places an order with Indus. If a tower already stands there, Indus adds the operator as a new 'co-location' (tenant) – it mounts the antennas, adds power and cabinet space and starts billing within weeks. If not, Indus builds a new tower (analysts cite ₹20–25 lakh per tower, a figure management did not dispute) with that operator as the anchor tenant.

Rent is set per tenant under the MSA. In Q4 FY26 a tower earned ₹66,604 a month in sharing revenue, or ₹41,078 per tenant. The first tenant largely pays back the tower; the second and third tenants pay a similar rent but need almost no extra capex, which is why the sharing factor (tenants per tower, 1.63 in Q2 FY27) is the single most important number for returns.

Contracts are long: new tenancies and renewals carry a minimum 10-year tenure, with built-in escalation of about 2.5% a year that covers most cost inflation. Lock-in and exit penalties make it expensive for an operator to walk away early, though at renewal Indus sometimes gives discounts, and lean (low-cost) rural towers earn much lower rent (₹16,535 per tenant per month).

Energy is a separate bill. Indus runs grid connections, batteries, solar panels and diesel generators at the site and charges operators either a fixed rate per tenant or actuals (diesel is billed on actuals with no lag). Because the recovery rates are fixed and real consumption varies, the energy line runs slightly negative; Indus improves it by cutting diesel use (down 11% YoY in Q2 FY27) and adding solar (49,000 sites).

Billing is monthly. The main cash risk is the customer's ability to pay: Vodafone Idea's past shortfalls forced large provisions, later written back (₹5,100 cr reversed in FY25). The business generates heavy free cash flow (₹3,760 cr in FY26), which the board now pays out as dividend (₹14/share final for FY26).

Growth comes from operators adding 4G/5G sites and tenancies; Indus added about 15,200 towers and 22,500 co-locations in FY26. It has begun building towers in Zambia, Uganda and Nigeria with Airtel Africa as anchor tenant, funded mainly with debt; economics are not yet disclosed.

534816.costs: The cost base is mostly fixed once a tower stands: site rent to landowners (now booked as lease depreciation and interest, about ₹4,300 cr in FY26), maintenance (₹1,467 cr) and staff (₹878 cr) barely move when a second tenant is added. The largest expense, power and fuel (₹11,996 cr, about 83% of operating costs), is largely passed through to operators. The business is capital-heavy – FY26 capex was ₹8,817 cr, about 70% for growth and 25% for replacement such as batteries and generators – and lease liabilities stood at ₹20,206 cr in March 2026, though excluding leases Indus held net cash of ₹4,932 cr. Operating leverage comes from tenancy: every extra tenant on an existing tower adds rent with little extra cost, which is why EBITDA margin (55% in FY26) sits far above that of the operators who pay it.
moat: Scale: about 2.7 lakh macro towers and 4.4 lakh tenancies – the largest tower portfolio in India – which is hard to replicate because new sites need land, permits and years to build.
Network effect of sharing: an existing tower with spare capacity is cheaper for an operator to join than building its own, so incumbents win most co-locations.
Long contracts: minimum 10-year tenure with escalators and exit penalties make revenue sticky and visible.
Promoter alignment: Bharti Airtel owns just over half of Indus and is its largest tenant, anchoring both new orders and the Africa expansion.

Core rental revenue tracks these counts
The economic heart of the business, excluding the energy pass-through
Shows energy losses and tenancy leverage together
Funds dividends; the board distributes FCF
Lower diesel narrows the negative energy margin

financials.note: PAT fell 28% YoY because FY25 included a ₹5,100 cr receivables write-back; normalised PAT grew about 13%.

risks: Customer concentration: three operators are effectively the whole market, and Vodafone Idea's finances decide whether its tenancies grow, shrink or go unpaid.
Renewals: as old tenancies expire, operators can negotiate discounts or exit; one tenancy agreement has expired and is still under discussion.
Energy pass-through mismatch: fixed recovery rates against volatile diesel and grid prices keep the energy margin negative.
Operator self-builds or rival towercos (e.g., Jio's own infrastructure) can take new tenancies away from Indus.
Africa expansion is debt-funded, in new currencies and regulatory regimes, with unit economics not yet disclosed.

539871.name: Thyrocare Technologies Ltd
539871.summary: Thyrocare is a wholesale pathology lab: it rarely deals with patients directly. About 12,900 independent franchisees (small labs, clinics and collection points) and partners such as PharmEasy, insurers and health-tech apps collect blood samples and send them to Thyrocare's 48 labs, paying it per test from a published business-to-business rate card. Huge volume (≈5.5 crore tests a quarter) at about ₹40 per test lets it be the low-cost processor for other people's patients.

streams.how: Franchisees buy tests at Thyrocare's published rate card, with volume-based slabs, and charge their own patients what they choose; Thyrocare processes and reports.
streams.driver: Active franchisees (12,911) × revenue per franchisee (≈₹1.2 lakh/quarter)

streams.how: Larger accounts (PharmEasy about 11% of the segment, insurers, health-tech, camps) send volumes at negotiated discounts; incremental tests in a panel are often discounted.

mechanics: A patient walks into a small neighbourhood lab or clinic that is a Thyrocare franchisee. The franchisee draws blood, sells the test or package (for example the Aarogyam preventive panels, about a third of pathology revenue) at its own retail price, and ships the sample to the nearest Thyrocare lab; the company says one is within 150 km anywhere in India.

Thyrocare bills the franchisee, not the patient, at a published rate card with volume discounts. The franchisee's profit is the gap between what it charges the patient and Thyrocare's rate. Thyrocare does not raise prices to grow: FY27 growth is guided as about 75% volume and 25% mix, and it cut biochemistry prices in Q4 FY26 to pull in more tests.

Partners such as PharmEasy, insurers and health-tech apps bring their own customers, often through software (API) links. They pay negotiated prices; PharmEasy has historically had a 15% discount to the rate card, approved as a related-party deal because both belong to the API Holdings group.

Labs run high-throughput automated analysers overnight. Realisation is low per test (about ₹40) but a patient buys about 10 tests at once, giving about ₹404 of revenue per patient. New specialty tests (allergy, genomics such as NIPT) fetch around ₹1,000 each and are about 4% of pathology revenue.

Growth is mainly about adding franchisees (1,500–2,000 a year guided; about 1,180 added in Q2 FY27) since revenue per franchisee has stayed flat for about 12 quarters. Extra volume is processed in existing labs running at about 65% utilisation, which is where the operating leverage comes from.

Distribution through 12,900 franchisees, 80% beyond Tier 1 cities, which rivals would need years of field work to replicate.
Lab density (a lab within 150 km anywhere, average turnaround about 3.5 hours, 96–97% of samples in NABL-accredited labs) supports quality and speed.
Being a B2B supplier rather than a consumer brand means it can serve competing front-ends, including PharmEasy and insurers.

540750.name: Indian Energy Exchange Ltd
540750.summary: IEX runs India's dominant electricity spot market: power buyers (mostly state distribution companies and industries) and sellers (generators) both pay IEX a fee of up to 2 paise for every unit (kWh) that clears. It never owns the power; it matches bids, clears and settles the money, and keeps 96% of revenue from these per-unit fees with ~84% margins. The big risk is regulatory: CERC's 'market coupling' and fee review could erode its 99% share or its fee.

payers.who: Buyers: state DISCOMs (~80% of buy volume), 5,300+ industrial consumers, open-access users
payers.pays: Transaction fee per unit bought (cap 2 paise/kWh)

payers.who: Sellers: generators, renewable developers, traders, obligated entities selling RECs
payers.pays: Transaction fee per unit sold (cap 2 paise/kWh) and per certificate traded

payers.pays: Annual subscription, membership and processing fees

outflows.gets: Power payments collected from buyers and paid out on settlement

₹14 cr technology and ₹12 cr legal/professional (FY26), legal up on the market-coupling litigation
Dividends and a buyback under evaluation, funded by ~₹1,400 cr net worth

streams.name: Transaction fees (electricity and certificates)
streams.basis: FY26 standalone revenue from operations (₹608 cr)
streams.how: A per-unit fee charged to both buyer and seller on every MWh cleared in the Day-Ahead, Real-Time, Term-Ahead and Green markets, and a per-certificate fee on RECs. FY26 transaction fees ₹584 cr.
streams.driver: Units cleared (141 BU in FY26) × fee per unit

streams.name: Annual subscription and membership fees
streams.how: Yearly subscription paid by members and participants (₹22.8 cr) plus small membership/processing fees (₹1.2 cr).
streams.driver: Number of members and registered participants (9,100+)

streams.how: Issues international renewable energy certificates for a per-certificate fee; revenue ₹7.7 cr in FY26.
streams.driver: I-REC issuance (179 lakh in FY26)

streams.name: IGX gas exchange (47.3% associate)
streams.how: IGX earns its own per-trade gas fees (₹61 cr revenue, ₹42 cr PAT in FY26); IEX books its share of profit below revenue. Stake to fall to 25% via IPO.
streams.driver: Gas volume (76.8 mn MMBtu FY26)

mechanics: Each day participants submit buy and sell bids for each 15-minute block of the next day (Day-Ahead Market, DAM) or for half-hour windows an hour ahead (Real-Time Market, RTM). IEX's algorithm finds one clearing price per block; every cleared buyer pays that price and every cleared seller receives it. Grid-India then schedules the power. The Term-Ahead Market (TAM) offers daily to monthly contracts, and the Green market does the same for renewable power.

IEX earns only the fee, not the power price. CERC caps the fee at 2 paise per kWh per side; IEX's blended realisation is about ₹0.036–0.037 per unit (both sides combined, per management), so a ₹5.72/unit DAM price in Q2 FY27 means the exchange earns well under 1% of the transaction value. Revenue therefore rises with volume, not with power prices, although high prices can push buyers toward bilateral deals and reduce exchange volume.

Payment security is built in: buyers must pay in (or keep margins) before delivery, IEX's clearing function pays sellers the following day, and a settlement guarantee fund backs defaults. This removes the DISCOM credit risk that plagues the rest of Indian power, and it is a key reason generators prefer selling on the exchange.

Volume growth comes from more generators and buyers using short-term markets: exchange volume grew 17% in FY26 against roughly 1% power-demand growth, and RTM (now ~42% of volume) is the fastest-growing segment. Management expects ~15% volume growth in FY27 and more storage (batteries) and merchant renewables to trade on the exchange.

Almost all costs are fixed (people, IT, rent), so each extra unit traded is nearly pure profit. IEX also holds sizeable treasury investments that produced ₹137 cr of other income in FY26, about a fifth of total income.

There is no cost of goods, as power money is a pass-through. Operating leverage is high: volume growth of 14–17% a year translates into slightly faster profit growth, held back only by rising legal and regulatory spend.
moat: Liquidity network effect: 99%+ share of DAM and RTM; a single clearing price is only meaningful where most bids sit, so rival exchanges PXIL and HPX have stayed marginal there.
Participant base: 9,100+ registered participants, 800–900 active daily, and 70%+ of cleared volume through API links built into DISCOM and generator systems.
Benchmark price: IEX DAM/RTM prices are used in contracts, regulatory filings and the SECI CfD pilot, reinforcing its central role.
Licensed and regulated: power exchanges need CERC registration and clearing infrastructure; capacity to add products (Green RTM, peak contracts, coal exchange) sits with incumbents.

Fee regulation: CERC is reportedly considering cutting the fee to about 1.5 paise per unit (1.25 for TAM) from the 2 paise cap; with 96% of revenue from this fee, a cut would hit revenue roughly in proportion.
Buyer concentration and policy: DISCOMs are ~80% of buy volume and the top buyers account for 50–60%; state policy or long-term PPAs can shift volume off-exchange.
Price spikes and supply shocks: in tight months, price caps and bilateral contracting reduce DAM volume (DAM grew only 2–5% a year since 2020).

542597.name: MSTC Ltd
542597.summary: MSTC is a government-owned online auction house. Ministries, PSUs, state governments and private companies use its platform to sell scrap, end-of-life vehicles, iron ore, coal, mineral blocks, land and even liquor licences, and MSTC earns a small service fee on each sale. It takes a fraction of a percent of about ₹80,000 cr of annual transactions and holds no inventory, so it runs at a ~68% EBITDA margin with almost no capital. Rules that push public bodies to auction rather than negotiate are what bring in the business.

payers.who: Ministries and state governments
payers.pays: Fees for running coal/mineral block auctions, land and liquor-licence auctions, e-procurement and custom portals (e.g. DGFT gold-quota portal)

streams.name: Scrap and end-of-life vehicle e-auctions
streams.how: Sellers list ferrous and non-ferrous scrap, surplus stores and scrapped vehicles; registered buyers bid online and MSTC earns a service charge on the realised sale.
streams.driver: Scrap prices (up ~8–10% a quarter recently) × volumes; ELV flows under vehicle-scrappage and EPR rules (~2 lakh vehicles in FY26)

streams.name: Minerals and coal (incl. block auctions)
streams.how: Iron ore, pellets, chrome ore and coal are sold lot by lot through MSTC auctions; it also runs government auctions of mineral and commercial coal blocks for a fee.
streams.driver: Iron ore volumes (1.54 mn tonnes in Q2 FY27), Coal India e-auction volumes, number of block tranches

streams.name: Other e-sales, portals and services
streams.basis: Rest of e-commerce revenue; not split out
streams.how: Land parcels, liquor licences, oil rigs and surplus assets for state bodies, plus software, AMC (annual maintenance) and custom portals, priced per event or per contract.
streams.driver: New government clients and one-off mandates (e.g. ₹2,850 cr Karnataka land auctions)

streams.name: E-procurement
streams.how: Fees from buyers' procurement tenders run on MSTC's platform.
streams.driver: PSU procurement routed via MSTC rather than GeM or others

mechanics: A PSU, say a steel plant or railway zone, signs up with MSTC to dispose of scrap. MSTC catalogues the lots, publishes the auction, registers and verifies bidders and collects their earnest money deposits (EMDs), then runs a live online bidding session. The highest bidder wins, pays, and lifts the material. MSTC's revenue is its service charge, not the sale value, and it never owns the goods.

Pricing is set per scheme and client. For Coal India spot e-auctions, each bidder pays a ₹20 per tonne process fee on the quantity it bids for. Scrap and mineral sales carry service charges agreed with the seller. Management says 30–40% or more of e-auction business is won in competitive bidding against other platforms; the rest comes by allocation from government and PSU clients.

The take rate is tiny but the base is huge. FY26 gross value transacted was ₹79,737 cr against ₹359.3 cr revenue, a blended ≈0.45% (est.). H1 FY27 GTV was ₹54,580 cr on ₹204.3 cr revenue (≈0.37%, est.). Revenue therefore follows the value and volume of what clients sell: scrap and iron-ore prices, Coal India's auction quantity, and how many mineral blocks the government auctions.

Cash: buyer deposits and sale proceeds pass through MSTC before reaching sellers, so its cash balance swings with timing (up ~70% at Sep 2026 vs March). Interest on this cash and reserves gives large other income (₹121.8 cr in FY26, about a quarter of total income), which lifts reported profit well above operating profit.

Strategy is moving from trading to pure platform. MSTC used to buy and resell goods for clients backed by a 110% bank guarantee, which was low margin and carried credit risk. That business was fully exited by Q1 FY27 and FSNL, its scrap-handling subsidiary, was sold in FY25. New platforms (TReDS invoice discounting with RBI in-principle approval, an EPR certificate exchange, a travel portal) are designed to earn per-transaction fees on existing infrastructure, but none has produced revenue yet.

543232.name: Computer Age Management Services Ltd
543232.summary: CAMS is the back office for most Indian mutual funds: as registrar and transfer agent (RTA) it processes every purchase, redemption and SIP, and keeps investor records for about two-thirds of industry assets. Asset managers (AMCs), not investors, pay it, mostly a small basis-point fee on the assets it services, so revenue rises with markets and SIP inflows while a near-duopoly with KFintech keeps switching rare.

payers.who: Mutual fund AMCs (~31 houses, incl. 9 of the 15 largest)
payers.pays: Annual fee as basis points of average AUM serviced (tiered), plus per-transaction, NFO, call-centre and other charges

payers.who: Merchants, fintechs, insurers and AMCs using CAMSPay
payers.pays: Payment gateway/aggregator fees per transaction

payers.who: AIF and PMS managers
payers.pays: Fund administration and investor servicing fees

₹500 cr re-architecture programme (about ₹290 cr capitalised) plus ~₹75 cr on-prem capex a year
High payout; FY26 dividends ~₹305 cr

streams.name: MF asset-based fees
streams.how: Each AMC pays an annual rate in basis points of the average AUM CAMS services, with 'telescopic' slabs that fall as assets grow; equity carries a higher rate than debt and far higher than passive funds (~0.5 bp).
streams.driver: Serviced AUM (₹58.5 lakh cr) × blended yield (~2.1 bp est.)

streams.name: MF non-asset-based fees
streams.how: Charges per transaction or per service: NFO processing, SIP registrations, call centre, MF Central and other investor services.
streams.driver: Transaction counts, NFO activity

streams.how: Payment gateway and aggregator fees on mandates, UPI and card payments for AMCs, insurers and other merchants; revenue base ~₹100 cr a year, growing 50%+.
streams.driver: Payment volumes; card mix lowers margins

streams.name: AIF / alternatives servicing
streams.how: Fund administration, investor onboarding and reporting for AIFs and PMS under service mandates; ~50% of the outsourced market. Management calls it services-heavy (~20% margin).
streams.driver: AIF AUM serviced (₹3.3 lakh cr)

streams.name: KRA, insurance repository, Think360 and others
streams.how: Fees per KYC record uploaded or fetched (rates cut ~29–30% in Apr 2026), e-insurance account fees, account-aggregator and analytics/SaaS fees.
streams.driver: New investor KYCs, policy dematerialisation

mechanics: When an investor buys a mutual fund through an app, a distributor or directly, the transaction lands at the fund's RTA. CAMS validates the application and KYC, creates or updates the folio, processes payment, allots units at that day's NAV, and handles redemptions, SIP debits, statements, tax certificates and compliance reports. The investor pays CAMS nothing; the AMC pays out of its own fee income.

Contracts with AMCs run multiple years and are priced mainly as basis points on AUM. Rates are telescopic: as a fund house's AUM crosses thresholds the marginal rate falls, so CAMS's blended yield drifts down about 2–3% a year even without a price cut. Mix also matters: debt pays ~2–2.25 bp, passive funds ~0.5 bp, equity more, so a shift to index funds dilutes yield.

Because ~74% of revenue is tied to AUM, revenue grows with both net inflows (SIPs, where CAMS has a ~64% collection share) and market moves. A 10% fall in equity markets cuts asset-based revenue with only a short lag, while most costs stay.
Fees are computed on average AUM serviced and billed to large, creditworthy AMCs, so receivables are low-risk; the company held ~₹900 cr of cash in Sep 2026 after paying dividends.
Non-MF businesses (~16% of revenue) are growing 20%+ but at ~19% EBITDA margin versus ~46% for the group. Payments, AIF, KYC and insurance repository reuse the same investor-servicing infrastructure.

Most are semi-fixed, so when AUM grows ~12–15% and costs grow under 10%, margins widen 100–200 bp a year. CAMS is cutting headcount (~250–300 fewer in FY27) through AI-based form processing, while a ₹500 cr cloud re-architecture lifts depreciation for several years. Switching costs: moving an AMC means migrating crores of folios, SIP mandates and years of records under SEBI scrutiny, so moves are rare and slow.
Network position: thousands of distributors, MF Central and transaction integrators plug into CAMS's systems.
Regulatory compliance: SEBI-mandated investments in cybersecurity and resilience (several hundred crore) raise the bar for new entrants.

543328.name: Krsnaa Diagnostics Ltd
543328.summary: Krsnaa runs CT/MRI scanning centres and pathology labs inside government hospitals under public-private partnerships (PPP): it wins a state tender, puts in the machines and staff at its own cost, and is then paid a fixed rate per test – usually by the state government, which gives the tests free to patients. Its prices are 60–80% below private-market rates, so profit comes from huge volumes (59 million tests in FY26) and low cost per test. A small but fast-growing retail arm sells tests directly to consumers.

payers.who: State governments and health missions (e.g., Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Punjab, Himachal, Karnataka)
payers.pays: Reimbursement per test at the tender rate for free tests given to government-hospital patients (≈63% est.: the remainder after management's 35–38% cash-based share, Q2 FY27)

payers.who: Patients paying cash at PPP centres and retail customers (RPL)
payers.pays: Government-approved or Krsnaa's own low rates per test at the counter; retail is about 9% of revenue (35–38% cash-based share, Q2 FY27)

outflows.gets: Large on-site workforce (≈4,000–5,000 people added for Rajasthan alone)
Reagents per test; CT/MRI machines (planned capitalisation ≈₹500 cr in FY27)
Fees/revenue share, ≈₹41 cr in Q1 FY27 and rising with Rajasthan
Interest on a ₹430 cr ADB debenture (7.79%) and term loans; finance cost ₹34 cr in FY26

streams.name: Radiology (CT, MRI, X-ray, PET-CT, teleradiology)
streams.how: Krsnaa installs scanners in district hospitals and medical colleges and is paid per scan at the tender rate (e.g., a CT brain at about ₹973 vs ₹3,500+ privately, per a 2023 broker comparison). Contracts typically run 10+ years.
streams.driver: Machines installed × scans per machine per day × rate per scan

streams.name: Pathology (blood and lab tests)
streams.how: Hub-and-spoke labs and collection centres in government facilities, paid per test at tender rates; contracts typically 5+ years. Rajasthan, the largest new contract, covers 31 mother labs, 62 hub labs and 1,228 collection centres.
streams.driver: Collection centres × tests per patient × rate per test

streams.name: Retail (Krsnaa Pathology/RPL, included in the above)
streams.how: Consumers pay directly at franchise and company collection points (3,500+ touchpoints); about ₹60 cr or ~8% of FY26 revenue, ~9% in H1 FY27. Targeted at 20%+ of revenue in 2–3 years.
streams.driver: Touchpoints × patient footfall × spend per visit

mechanics: A state health department floats a tender for diagnostics at its hospitals. Krsnaa bids a rate card per test – winners tend to be the lowest bidder with a track record – and if it wins, it signs a long contract: about 10+ years for radiology and 5+ years for pathology, with annual or biennial escalation of 2–5%. CGHS rate revisions do not reprice existing tenders.

The government provides space in its hospital; Krsnaa procures, finances, installs and runs the machines, labs, IT and staff. This shifts the capex burden off the state, which is why Krsnaa's balance sheet carries the scanners (depreciation ₹90 cr in FY26).

Patients referred by government doctors usually get tests free; Krsnaa bills the state monthly at the agreed rate per test. In some contracts (Punjab PET-CT, Himachal CT) patients pay cash at the counter at government-approved rates instead – these 'cash PPPs' were 35–38% of revenue in Q2 FY27 and are targeted at 40–45% by FY27 end because they avoid payment delays.

Collection is the bottleneck: states pay slowly, so receivable days were about 139 at end-FY26 and receivables climbed to about ₹470 cr by September 2026 as Rajasthan billing cycles bedded in. Krsnaa targets 90–120 days.

Economics depend on volume. Prices are 60–80% below private chains, but a scanner or lab that runs near capacity covers its fixed staff and depreciation and then earns high incremental margins. New contracts drag margins for several quarters: Rajasthan's staff and labs were in place before volumes arrived, pulling EBITDA margin to 25–27% in Q1–Q2 FY27 from 29% a year earlier. Management sees Rajasthan at about ₹250 cr annualised revenue at maturity, mostly in FY28.
Retail uses the same labs: spare capacity built for PPP volumes processes higher-priced consumer tests, which is why management wants retail to reach a double-digit share of revenue.

543328.costs: Most costs are fixed per site once a contract starts: on-site technicians and doctors, rent-free but staffed collection centres, machine maintenance, depreciation (₹90 cr, about 12% of FY26 revenue) and interest on the debt used to buy equipment (₹34 cr). Variable costs are reagents and consumables per test and the fees paid to host hospitals and channel partners, which have grown with Rajasthan. Capex intensity is high for a services company – about ₹500 cr of capitalisation is planned for FY27 – and debt-to-equity rose to 0.53x in FY26 after the ADB debenture. Operating leverage is strong as utilisation of each scanner and lab rises, but every new contract first dilutes margins and stretches working capital.
moat: Scale and track record in PPP: 196 CT/MRI centres, 259 pathology labs and thousands of collection centres across 19 states and UTs (Q2 FY27) – tenders favour bidders who have delivered before.
Lowest-cost operator: centralised labs and high volumes let it bid 60–80% below market while keeping margins comparable to listed peers.
Long contracts: 5–10+ year tenures give a reported ₹6,000–7,000 cr of revenue visibility over 5–7 years.
Rural reach: about 75% of centres are in rural areas where private chains are scarce.

543470.name: Softtech Engineers Ltd
543470.summary: Softtech sells software that lets city governments approve building plans and permits online (CivitPERMIT, used in 1,500+ cities across 18 states), plus tools to monitor infrastructure projects and run Mumbai's electronic exchange for development rights. Most money still comes as one-time project fees from government buyers, but a growing slice is recurring: subscriptions, maintenance and per-transaction fees, including 0.5% of the value of every TDR trade in Mumbai.

payers.who: State governments, municipal bodies and public agencies (e.g. Airport Authority of India)
payers.pays: One-time software licence and implementation fees under tendered projects, often paid in milestones with retentions

payers.who: Same clients plus permit applicants, developers and private AEC firms
payers.pays: Recurring fees: SaaS subscriptions, annual maintenance (AMC) and pay-per-use transaction fees, including 0.5% of each Mumbai TDR trade

German subsidiary, US partner and sales hires

streams.name: CivitPERMIT (building and land permit automation)
streams.how: Won through state or city tenders: a licence and implementation fee to automate plan scrutiny against building codes, then AMC or subscription, and in some projects a fee per application processed.
streams.driver: New state/city contracts + permit volumes on live transaction-based projects

streams.name: CivitINFRA (project monitoring)
streams.how: Project-management software for public works agencies, sold as licence plus AMC; e.g. a ~₹17 cr Airport Authority of India order, ~40% recognised in FY26 and the rest over ~3 years.
streams.driver: Government infra programmes and large one-off orders

streams.name: CivitBUILD, BIM/GIS services and others
streams.how: Construction ERP for private builders, BIM and GIS services (some overseas), and newer AI/digital-twin products, sold as licences, subscriptions or service fees.
streams.driver: Private and overseas customer wins

streams.name: CivitTDR (Mumbai e-TDR exchange)
streams.how: Developers buying and selling Transfer of Development Rights (TDR, extra buildable floor area granted to landowners) must trade on the BMC platform since 10 May 2026; Softtech earns a transaction fee capped at 0.5% of trade value.
streams.driver: TDR trade value in Mumbai (≈₹8,000 cr in FY26) × 0.5%

mechanics: The core customer is a government body that must give building permissions. Softtech's engine reads an architect's drawing, checks it against local building bylaws and routes approvals online, cutting approval times. A state or city buys this through a tender; Softtech says it wins about 70% of bids it chooses to pursue and loses mostly on price.

A typical deal has a large one-time part (licence, customisation, rollout) recognised as milestones are met, then a recurring tail of AMC, hosting/SaaS or per-application fees. In FY26 one-time revenue was about two-thirds of standalone sales and recurring about one-third; SaaS and pay-per-use revenue was ₹31.7 cr (+38.6%). The company is pushing clients toward subscription and per-transaction pricing.

Getting paid is the slow part. Government payments follow approvals and budgets, retentions can be held for years, and debtor days were 260 in FY26 (372 in FY25). So reported EBITDA (24% margin) turns into far less cash and profit after interest and amortisation; FY26 PAT was only ₹5.3 cr.

The TDR exchange is a different, platform-style model. In Mumbai, landowners who give land for public use receive TDR certificates that builders buy to construct extra floors. BMC made its e-TDR platform, built and run by Softtech, mandatory from 10 May 2026; Softtech takes up to 0.5% of each trade. On FY26 trade value of about ₹8,000 cr that implies roughly ₹40 cr of revenue a year at 70-80% margins (management estimate), if volumes move fully onto the platform.

Order book was about ₹220 cr (Q1 FY27) against a pipeline of about ₹490 cr; management expects about 60% of the order book to turn into revenue within a year and targets ₹300 cr revenue by FY29 at 28-30% EBITDA margin, with overseas (Germany, US, Middle East) rising toward half of revenue.

streams.name: Trust Services (DSC, eSign, tokens)
streams.how: As a Certifying Authority licensed by India's Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA), eMudhra issues DSCs sold per certificate, usually with a USB crypto token, plus Aadhaar-based eSign charged per signature. Most sales go through partners and its portal.
streams.driver: Regulatory filings that require DSCs, eSign volumes (7–8 lakh a day), token supply

mechanics: Trust services: DSCs are needed for income-tax and company (ROC) filings, foreign trade, e-tenders and banking documents, and every company director must sign filings digitally. eMudhra, a CCA-licensed Certifying Authority since 2008, verifies the applicant's identity and issues a time-limited certificate. Sales go mostly through a network of chartered accountants, company secretaries and resellers. The certificate itself is high-margin; the USB token bundled with it is a pass-through with ~10% gross margin. Because certificates expire, users come back to renew.

Enterprise solutions grew out of that know-how: the same PKI that runs eMudhra's own CA is sold to central banks, national certifying authorities (e.g. Nigeria's regulator), banks and governments that want to run their own. It is packaged as emCA (sovereign PKI), CertiNext (certificate lifecycle management), SecurePass (identity, MFA and privileged access) and emSigner (e-signature workflows). Revenue comes as licence plus implementation upfront, then annual maintenance or subscription; 65% of total business is recurring.

Geography and channel: 36% India, 34% North America, 12% Europe, 11% Middle East & Africa, 7% APAC in FY26. 60% is sold direct and 40% via partners. Data centres in India, the US, Europe and UAE meet data-residency rules. The CRYPTAS acquisition gave a European base and eIDAS credentials. It is now replacing third-party CLM software with eMudhra's own, which should lift margins.

Deal flow is lumpy. Large government and bank orders are recognised as they are delivered, so quarters swing (India enterprise dipped in Q4 FY26 after a large Q3 defence deal). The product order book was ₹238 cr at FY26 end. Payment terms on government projects stretch receivables, and FY26 operating cash flow was ₹133 cr against ₹110 cr PAT.

In October 2026, private keys behind eight intermediate certificates in eMudhra's publicly trusted TLS (website certificate) hierarchy were compromised. Mozilla and Google removed the affected root, and eMudhra exited global TLS sales. That line was only ~1% of revenue, but FY27 guidance was cut to ~₹800 cr total income and ~₹125 cr PAT because of the reputational spillover. The episode shows that in this business, trust is the product.

543591.name: Dreamfolks Services Ltd
543591.summary: DreamFolks is a middleman: banks and card networks pay it to deliver the travel perks printed on their cards (airport lounges, golf, airport transfers, spa, dining), and it pays the lounges and service providers that actually serve the cardholder, keeping a thin spread. Until 2025 almost all revenue came from Indian domestic airport lounges; that business collapsed when banks cut free lounge access and the big lounge operators (Adani, Encalm, TFS-linked Semolina) stopped serving it, so revenue halved in FY26 and the company is rebuilding around global lounges, railway lounges it runs itself, and lifestyle benefits.

Upfront minimum guarantees to secure access (one-off payment in Q1 FY27)

streams.how: When a cardholder enters a partner lounge, DreamFolks bills the card network or bank an agreed per-visit fee and pays the lounge operator its own per-visit rate; the difference is its margin. After exiting Indian domestic lounges in Sept 2025, volume is mostly overseas (1,100+ lounges, with ETT in Dubai).
streams.driver: Eligible cardholders × visits × spread per visit

streams.name: Golf, railway lounges, lifestyle and memberships
streams.how: Golf games and lessons, meet-and-assist, transfers, spa, dining and other perks billed to banks per use; railway lounges (Chennai, Mumbai, Vadodara, Nashik) run directly via Ten11 and paid by walk-ins or programmes; DF Club paid memberships.

mechanics: The real customer is the card issuer or network, not the traveller. A bank promises 'free lounge access' on a card; DreamFolks integrates with the bank's card data, verifies eligibility when the card is swiped at the lounge desk (the traveller pays little or nothing), and later bills the network or bank. India-issued cards were about 80% of domestic lounge entries at the IPO, and DreamFolks handled most of them.

On the other side it has contracts with lounge operators that set what it pays per guest. The model owns no lounges at airports, so it needs little capital, but the margin is only the spread: gross margin was about 11-12% (FY25 ₹150 cr gross profit on ₹1,292 cr revenue; FY26 ₹74 cr on ₹661 cr).

That thin spread proved fragile. In FY26 banks moved from unlimited free visits to spend-based access, Axis Bank and ICICI Bank programmes closed from 1 July 2025, and suppliers Adani Digital, Semolina Kitchens and Encalm Hospitality ended their arrangements; DreamFolks discontinued domestic airport lounge services for certain clients from 16 Sept 2025. Revenue fell from ₹1,292 cr (FY25) to ₹661 cr (FY26) and ₹70 cr in H1 FY27.

The rebuild has two parts. Asset-light: selling more benefits (global lounges, golf, transfers, spa, coffee offers, flight-cancellation cover with Mastercard) into the same bank integrations. Asset-heavier: owning and operating railway lounges through Ten11 Hospitality (50.01% stake), where it earns the full lounge fee but must spend capex and deposits; management targets ₹500 cr revenue in 5 years if it reaches at least 50 lounges.

Banks pay on credit after monthly reconciliation, while lounges are paid per visit, so receivables matter (about ₹130 cr at Dec 2025). Overseas lounges sometimes demand upfront minimum guarantees, which turned gross profit negative in Q4 FY26 and Q1 FY27.

543591.costs: Cost of services (payments to lounges and providers) is almost entirely variable and was about 89% of FY26 revenue, so the business only works at large volume. Below gross profit sit payroll, technology and new-business costs that are largely fixed; with revenue down about 90% from the FY26 peak quarter, these fixed costs now exceed gross profit, producing EBITDA losses. Capital intensity was near zero historically but is rising with railway lounges (₹1.5-6 cr each), the ETT acquisition (about ₹36 cr for 60.24%) and global minimum guarantees. Operating leverage is strong in both directions.
moat: Integrations with Indian banks, card networks and OTAs, plus a contracted network of 1,100+ global lounges and 6,000+ touchpoints, that a new aggregator would take years to replicate.
Technology platform that lets banks design segmented, spend-based benefit programmes across many service types.
Railway lounge coverage via Ten11, an early position in station modernisation.
The moat proved weak in its core: lounge operators and banks could bypass the aggregator, which is the central lesson of FY26.

543638.summary: Tracxn sells annual subscriptions to a database of private companies (about 7.7 million profiled startups and private firms, their funding rounds, investors, financials and cap tables) to venture funds, investment banks, corporates and universities. Customers pay per seat, usually a year upfront, so cash arrives before revenue is booked. Almost all cost is the in-house team that builds the data, which makes profits very sensitive to whether revenue grows.

mechanics: Tracxn's analysts and software crawl about 980 million web domains, filings and news to build profiles of private companies, then tag them into sector 'feeds'. Prospects find it through free search traffic (6.2 million visits) and the free Tracxn Lite tier (285,000 sign-ups); there is no paid advertising.

A paying customer signs an annual licence priced by the number of seats (users), not by fund size or deals done. About 75% of FY26 billings were annual subscriptions, typically billed upfront, so cash lands first and revenue is recognised month by month; deferred revenue was ₹38.1 cr at Sept 2026, close to five months of revenue.

Average revenue is about ₹3.6 lakh per account per year and ₹1.3 lakh per user (Q1 FY27). It has drifted down from about ₹5 lakh per account as newer, smaller customers in new geographies join, even though list prices rose about 7%.

The model is renew-and-expand: revenue grows when accounts add seats, upgrade to more feeds or new teams sign on. Half of customers by count are investors and 45% corporates; investor demand tracks deal activity, which is why weak venture funding kept FY26 revenue flat at ₹84 cr.

Because the data team is a fixed cost, management says up to 80% of each extra rupee of revenue can reach EBITDA. In FY27 it chose to step up costs, nearly doubling closing-sales staff from 34 to about 60, pushing EBITDA negative until revenue catches up.

544088.name: Medi Assist Healthcare Services Ltd
544088.summary: Medi Assist is India's largest third-party administrator (TPA) – the back office that health insurers hire to issue cards, approve cashless hospital admissions and settle claims for the people they insure. It is paid by the insurer as a percentage of the premium (about 2.7% blended), so its revenue grows with India's health-insurance premiums without it taking any insurance risk. It also earns fees from government health schemes and is starting to sell its claims software to insurers per claim.

payers.pays: TPA fee as a % of the group premium administered, paid upfront and earned over the policy year

payers.who: State and central government health schemes
payers.pays: Administration fees under scheme contracts (16 states and UTs, 31 crore members)

payers.who: Health insurers for individual (retail) policies
payers.pays: TPA fee as a % of retail premium administered

payers.who: Insurers using its software, and international clients
payers.pays: Per-claim SaaS fees for the MAtrix platform (≈₹100–120 a claim) and overseas travel/expat claims fees

Purchased books such as Paramount TPA and Mayfair (international), integrated onto its platform

streams.how: Employers buy group health cover from an insurer and nominate Medi Assist to administer it; the insurer pays a fee fixed as a percentage of premium. Premium under administration crossed ₹23,000 cr in FY26 (market share 33.7%).
streams.driver: Group premium administered × fee % × retention (~93%)

streams.name: Government schemes
streams.how: Runs claims and hospital-network administration for state health schemes (PM-JAY-linked and state-funded) under multi-year contracts won by tender.
streams.driver: States won × members covered × contracted fee

streams.how: Administers individual policies for insurers that outsource retail claims; fee as % of premium (TPA-model retail premium ₹2,818 cr in FY26).
streams.driver: Retail premium administered × fee %

streams.name: International benefits administration
streams.how: Mayfair handles overseas medical and travel claims (claims from 141 countries, 21,000 providers) for a per-case or service fee.
streams.driver: Travel, student and expat case volumes

streams.how: Insurers that run claims in-house pay per claim to use Medi Assist's platform (base ≈₹100–120 a claim); add-ons like fraud and auto-adjudication could earn 5–10x more per claim but are not yet billed.
streams.driver: Claims processed on the platform × fee per claim

mechanics: When a company buys group health insurance, the employer picks both the insurer and the TPA. The insurer then pays Medi Assist a fee – about 2.7% of premium blended across group and retail – to issue e-cards, run a 24x7 helpdesk, approve cashless hospital admissions, check bills against its negotiated hospital rates, and settle or reimburse claims. Medi Assist never carries the claims risk; that stays with the insurer.

The fee is paid largely upfront when the policy starts, but revenue is recognised day by day (1/365) over the policy year. That creates a large contract liability (₹321.7 cr at September 2026) – customers' cash held before the work is done – and means revenue lags premium growth by two to three quarters.

Growth comes from three things: more premium per retained employer (same-store growth of about 7–9% as health costs and headcount rise), new employer wins, and acquisitions of rival TPA books (Paramount, completed and fully migrated by Q2 FY27). Retention normally runs at 93–94%; it dipped to about 90.5% in H1 FY27 after the Paramount transition.

Value to the insurer is cost control: in FY26 its MAven Guard fraud tool prevented over ₹540 cr of fraudulent claims and its hospital network delivered over ₹1,300 cr of discounts. That is what lets Medi Assist defend its fee as insurers squeeze expenses.

The newer model is software: insurers that do claims in-house rent MAtrix per claim, and AI modules can now be sold on top of insurers' own systems. Management hopes tech margins reach 1.5–2x the core TPA business, but this was only about 2.5% of FY26 revenue.

544088.costs: This is a people business: claims processors, in-house doctors, call-centre and hospital-desk staff make up the bulk of costs, and they scale with claim volumes and lives covered rather than premium, so rising medical inflation (bigger premiums per life) lifts revenue faster than cost. Technology is the second lever – AI auto-adjudication and the Paramount integration cut headcount by about 800 and pushed operating EBITDA margin from 17.1% in Q2 FY26 to 20.4% in Q2 FY27, against a 22–23% steady-state target. Capex is light, the company is debt-free with about ₹268 cr of cash, and the upfront-fee model means working capital is negative.
moat: Scale: largest TPA with about a third of group health premiums; a national hospital network and negotiated tariffs that small TPAs cannot match.
Regulatory licence: TPAs need IRDAI registration, and insurers are slow to move books once claims systems and hospital links are set up.
Data and fraud analytics trained on about a million claims a month, which improve the insurer's loss ratio.
Consolidator: proven ability to buy and migrate rival TPA books onto one platform.

544288.name: Black Buck Ltd (BlackBuck)
544288.summary: BlackBuck runs India's largest app for truck owners: about 9 lakh operators a month use it to pay tolls (FASTag), buy fuel, track their trucks and find loads. Most of its money does not come from truckers' pockets directly – banks and oil companies pay it a commission on the tolls and fuel that flow through the app – while truckers pay subscriptions for GPS devices and load listings. It is now layering higher-touch businesses on top: managed freight ('SuperLoads') and vehicle loans.

payers.pays: A commission equal to an agreed % of the toll and fuel value (GTV) routed through BlackBuck

payers.who: Truck operators and fleet owners
payers.pays: Telematics subscriptions (GPS, fuel sensors, dash-cams, AIS devices), load-board subscriptions and service fees (FASTag issuance, activation, recharge)

Acquisition spend and AI/product investment for growth businesses

streams.how: When a trucker recharges a FASTag or pays for fuel via BlackBuck, the partner bank or OMC pays BlackBuck an agreed percentage of that value. Tolling is about 90% of payments GTV (₹25,904 cr of ₹29,095 cr in FY26).
streams.driver: Payments GTV × take rate (not disclosed; management says unchanged QoQ)
