streams.how: Telematics customers pay an annual subscription for devices and software (over half collected in advance and recognised over time); loads-board users pay subscriptions; SuperLoads freight bills to shippers are booked here too, which inflates this line.
streams.driver: Active devices (≈5.07 lakh avg monthly) × annual fee; SuperLoads trips × freight

streams.name: Service fees
streams.how: One-off and recurring charges to truckers for FASTag issuance, replacement, activation and recharges, and other platform services.
streams.driver: New FASTags and active transacting operators

streams.name: Interest income on loans
streams.how: Interest on the small vehicle-finance book BlackBuck holds itself (about ₹60 cr of the ~₹600 cr managed with lending partners).
streams.driver: Own loan book × yield

mechanics: A truck owner downloads the BlackBuck app or meets one of about 10,000 offline touchpoints, gets a FASTag (increasingly issued on BlackBuck's own prepaid-payment licence, granted by RBI in July 2025) and starts recharging it through the app. Every toll swipe and fuel purchase earns BlackBuck a small cut paid by the bank or oil company, not by the trucker. In FY26, 67 crore payment transactions worth ₹29,095 cr passed through the platform.

Once on the app, operators are sold more services. Telematics is the second engine: a GPS or AIS (mandated tracking) device plus software, priced around ₹3,000–4,000 a year according to analyst checks. Over half of telematics revenue is collected in advance and recognised over the subscription period, so deferred revenue (up 56% YoY in Q2 FY27) is a lead indicator. First-year renewal is around 80% and rises in later years.

The marketplace started as a classifieds board where shippers and truckers pay a subscription to post and find loads (4.2 million loads posted in FY26). SuperLoads goes further: in 14 cities BlackBuck itself matches loads to trucks using AI, bills the shipper the full freight and pays the truck owner, keeping the spread. It runs on customer advances, so working capital is small, but gross revenue is large relative to margin.

Vehicle finance is mostly partner-led: banks and NBFCs lend to truckers BlackBuck sources and underwrites using its payment and GPS data, paying BlackBuck fees; only about a tenth of the ₹600 cr managed book sits on BlackBuck's balance sheet. Management expects it to break even at EBITDA level in FY27.

The core is very high-margin: contribution margin is about 93% because the commission arrives almost cost-free once a trucker is acquired. Cash comes in quickly – receivables are under three months in telematics and under 30 days elsewhere – and FY26 free cash flow (≈₹185–190 cr) roughly matched adjusted EBITDA.

What scales: payments and telematics ride road-freight growth, toll-rate inflation and state AIS mandates with little extra cost. What does not: SuperLoads needs city-by-city teams and is still in investment mode, which pulled incremental operating leverage down to about 50% from a historical 70–85%.

544311.name: International Gemological Institute (India) Ltd
544311.summary: IGI is paid a fee per grading report. Diamond growers, cutters, traders and jewellery makers send stones and pieces to its labs, and IGI issues a certificate on cut, colour, clarity and carat that buyers and retailers rely on. More than half the money comes from lab-grown diamond (LGD) makers, a segment where IGI is the default grader with about two-thirds of the market. That makes it a toll booth on the volume of LGD production rather than a bet on diamond prices.

streams.driver: AGL rollout to IGI labs worldwide

mechanics: A Surat grower polishes lab-grown stones and sends them to an IGI lab, often near its factory. Gemologists, helped by instruments and now AI-based scheduling, grade each stone on the 4Cs, laser-inscribe the report number and issue a report within about 2–3 days. The client pays a fee per report.

Pricing is per report and scales with stone size and service type. A certificate costs about 2–3% of an LGD's retail price, so buyers barely notice it, yet a stone without a recognised report is hard to sell to US retailers. That is the source of pricing power. Fees have not been raised structurally in recent quarters, so average realised price (ARP) moves with mix: ₹1,010 per report in Q1 FY27 (larger stones, AGL) and ₹891 in Q2 FY27 (more jewellery reports, which are cheaper).

Volume, not diamond prices, drives revenue. When LGD prices crashed (realisation down about 25% in Apr–May 2024), IGI's fee per report is not tied to stone value, so volumes kept growing. Management says the top 12–14 Indian growers make about 80% of India's LGD output and are adding capacity to roughly double in three years. IGI's top 8–10 growers give 40–50% of revenue.

India is the factory. The India entity earned ₹1,233.9 cr of the 15-month certification revenue at a ~73% EBITDA margin. Overseas labs in the US, Belgium, Dubai and elsewhere certify jewellery and natural stones close to retailers and pay or receive commissions within the group.

Cash conversion is strong: operating cash flow in H1 FY27 was ₹415.7 cr, 118% of PAT. Receivables fell to ₹240 cr, and the company held ₹1,075 cr of cash with no debt. Capex is small: lab space, grading machines and inscription lasers.

Employee cost was about ₹71–74 cr a quarter through CY25–Q1 CY26 and rising with hiring. Next come rent for lab space, marketing (brand and IPL sponsorship) and commissions paid to overseas subsidiaries. Equipment capex is small relative to revenue. Physical proximity: the largest LGD lab network sits near Surat's growers, and fast turnaround (2–3 days) matters to producers turning over inventory.

Asset-light, highly profitable model (~61% EBITDA, ~46% PAT margin) funds price competition and expansion without debt.

544439.name: Crizac Ltd
544439.summary: Crizac is a B2B platform that recruits international students for foreign universities, almost entirely in the UK. Students pay nothing: the universities pay Crizac a commission for every student who actually enrols and pays fees, and Crizac passes roughly two-thirds of that on to the thousands of local counselling agents who found the student. It is a toll on the international-student pipeline, with very little capital needed.

payers.pays: Commission per enrolled student, a share of the student's tuition, paid after enrolment and fee payment

payers.who: Universities in Ireland, New Zealand, Australia, the US and other destinations
payers.pays: Same per-student recruitment commission

payers.who: Lenders, accommodation and forex providers

outflows.gets: About 67–70% of revenue as agent commission, mostly paid directly in GBP
Lean team; salary cost guided at 3–4% of revenue over the medium term
Platform, EduMentor AI matching tool ($2.5m over five years)
Small bolt-on deals (StudiesPlanet, Global Tree, ForeignAdmits, Innova); dividends of ≥40% of PAT

streams.name: UK university recruitment commissions
streams.how: For each student who enrols, the university pays Crizac a commission linked to tuition; volume slabs and bonuses from top-ranked universities add to it. Crizac then pays its sub-agent's share.
streams.driver: Enrolments × tuition × commission rate (plus volume bonuses)

streams.name: Other destinations (Ireland, NZ, Australia, US, Netherlands)
streams.how: Same per-enrolment commission model; non-UK was 9.5% of H1 FY27 applications but only 1.4% of revenue so far. Target: 30% of revenue outside the UK by FY30.
streams.driver: Non-UK enrolments; acquisitions such as Medway (NZ) and Innova

streams.name: Value-added services and B2C counselling
streams.how: Referral fees for loans, visa prep, forex and accommodation (via ForeignAdmits) and direct student counselling (Global Tree). Guided to add 1–1.5% of revenue over a couple of years.
streams.driver: Attach rate of services to enrolled students

mechanics: A student in India, Nigeria, Pakistan or elsewhere walks into a local education counsellor. That counsellor (a 'sub-agent') logs the student onto Crizac's platform, which holds contracts with 600+ institutions and represents more than 95 of 100 UK commercial universities. Crizac's team checks documents, submits applications (a student typically applies to 2–2.5 universities) and supports the offer and visa process.

Nobody pays at the application stage. Only when the student enrols and pays tuition does the university pay Crizac a commission. Rates are confidential and set per university contract, with slabs and bonuses for hitting volume targets – which is why revenue per student fell in Q1 FY27 when fewer students went to high-fee top-ranked universities, even though enrolments rose 15%.

Crizac then pays the sub-agent who brought the student. In FY26 about two-thirds of revenue went out this way (gross margin 32.5%); in H1 FY27 the split was 30% retained and 70% paid out. Because universities pay in pounds and most agent payouts also go out in pounds, currency mainly affects the slice Crizac keeps – a weaker rupee (GBP/INR averaged 116 in FY26 vs 105) lifted margins by about 1–1.5 points.

Funnel economics: about 3.94 lakh applications in FY26 became 24,697 enrolments (blended conversion ≈14%; India ≈10%, China and Latin America ≈20%, Africa ≈5%). That works out to roughly ₹4.2 lakh of revenue per enrolled student (derived). Revenue is seasonal and follows UK intakes: Q4 (January intake) and Q2–Q3 (September) are large, Q1 is the trough.

The model needs almost no capital: no campuses, no real estate, no lending on its own book. FY26 ROCE was 48.6% and the company holds about ₹600 cr of net cash. The main things that scale are partner relationships and agent reach; what does not scale is regulatory exposure, since one country's visa policy drives nearly all revenue.

What is left is a small fixed base – staff (guided at 3–4% of revenue), technology and office costs – so EBITDA margins of 25–27% depend mostly on the retained share of commission and on currency. Capex is negligible (software was bought from a group company in FY24 and is being amortised; depreciation moved to straight-line from April 2026). Operating leverage is modest because most cost is agent payout, but every incremental bonus slab from a university drops almost entirely to profit.
moat: Two-sided network: contracts with 600+ institutions (including 95 of 100 UK commercial universities) on one side and 18,500+ counselling partners on the other; a new entrant needs both at once.
Long relationships: ties with the top 30 partners exceed five years, and the UK Agent Quality Framework raises compliance barriers that favour large, audited aggregators.
Source diversity: more than half of students now come from outside India (FY26 source mix: India 48.7%, rest of Asia 34.7%, Africa 16.4%).
Asset-light and cash-rich: high ROCE and net cash fund acquisitions into new corridors.

544443.name: Travel Food Services Ltd
544443.summary: Travel Food Services (TFS) wins long-term concessions to run food courts, quick-service restaurants and lounges inside Indian airports, then earns from travellers buying food and from banks, card networks and airlines paying for each lounge visit. Airports take a cut of sales (a percentage or a minimum guarantee, whichever is higher), but because each terminal has very few licensed F&B and lounge operators and passengers are captive, TFS earns about 85% gross margins and close to 40% EBITDA margins.

payers.pays: Menu prices for meals, coffee and snacks under 150+ partner and in-house brands

payers.who: Banks, card networks, airlines and loyalty programmes (plus walk-in guests)
payers.pays: A fee for each lounge visit their customers make, plus guests paying for upgrades and walk-in access

payers.pays: Management and other service fees for running their outlets

Royalties/franchise fees on partner-brand sales (partner brands were ~54% of FY25 QSR revenue)

streams.name: Lounges
streams.how: Most guests enter using a credit/debit card or airline status; the card network, bank or airline pays TFS a negotiated per-visit fee. Since Sept 2025 TFS contracts directly with banks and networks via its Eliteassist (EATS) platform instead of going through DreamFolks.
streams.driver: Eligible premium passengers × visits × per-visit rate, plus in-lounge upsell

streams.name: Management and other services
streams.how: Fees from unconsolidated JVs/associates (e.g. GHL at Hyderabad and Goa; Semolina at Adani airports) and passenger services such as meet-and-greet.
streams.driver: System-wide sales of JV units

mechanics: Everything starts with a tender. An airport operator auctions the right to run F&B or lounge space for 5 to 20 years (average 8.2 years at the IPO, about 6 years remaining). TFS bids a concession fee, usually a percentage of sales with a minimum annual guarantee (MAG), and commits to fit-out capex. Management says it bids for cash returns, not market share, and has renewed about 92% of expiring contracts.

Once a unit is open, the traveller pays at the till or the lounge desk. In food, TFS picks the brand mix (153 brands across 21 airports) to fill every price point. Partner brands like international coffee chains bring footfall but cost a royalty; in-house brands carry higher margins. Like-for-like sales normally grow 5 to 7 points faster than passenger traffic through premiumisation, combos and brand swaps.

In lounges, the passenger usually pays little or nothing; the bill goes to whoever gave the passenger the entitlement, mainly card networks and banks. Around 70-80% of Indian lounge entries are card-based. TFS used to receive many of these visits via aggregator DreamFolks, but ended that contract from 15 Sept 2025 after failing to agree terms and now bills banks and networks directly through EATS. This briefly pushed year-end receivables to about ₹264 cr, which management expects to normalise to 40-45 days by H1 FY27.

Reported revenue understates the business. System-wide sales (₹3,214 cr in FY26) include JV and associate outlets at big airports such as Hyderabad, Goa and the Adani airports, which are equity-accounted; only TFS's share of their profit and its management fees reach the consolidated P&L (₹1,650 cr revenue).

Cash is collected instantly in food (card/UPI at the till) and on credit from banks in lounges. The concession fee rises automatically with sales, so airports share in growth, while rent-like MAGs and staff are the fixed part that creates operating leverage when traffic rises and pain when it falls.

mechanics: An investor opens a demat account with a depository participant (DP), such as a bank or broker, which is connected to NSDL or to rival CDSL. NSDL holds the electronic record of ownership. Investors pay the DP, not NSDL, and DPs set their own retail tariffs. NSDL charges the DP a fixed ₹4 per debit (sale/transfer) instruction and fees per pledge, and the DP recovers these within its own charges.

Issuers are the other paying side and the more stable one. Every company whose securities sit in NSDL pays an annual custody fee of ₹11 per folio held with NSDL, plus a one-time joining fee (₹15,000–20,000), and pays per record when it runs a corporate action, IPO or e-voting. MCA rules requiring unlisted companies to dematerialise their shares drove ~63,000 new issuers in FY25–26, lifting custody fees 36% in FY26, but onboarding has slowed to ~6,500 in H1 FY27.

NSDL's strength is in value, not account count: it holds ~86% of demat custody value and 99.9% of FPI holdings because institutions, custodians and banks use it, but only ~4.7 cr of the industry's ~24 cr (est.) demat accounts. Retail accounts, mostly opened by discount brokers, have gone largely to CDSL; NSDL is winning back share in new accounts (17–18% incremental) via fintech DPs and fee waivers for young and women investors.

Fees are set by NSDL with SEBI's oversight and have barely moved for years; a request to raise issuer and settlement charges has been pending with the regulator for over a year. Growth therefore comes from volume (folios, issuers, transactions), not price.

The payments bank (95% owned) roughly doubles group revenue but contributes only ~10% of profit because most fees are passed to agents and partners. Standalone, NSDL earned ₹360.6 cr of FY26 PAT on ₹704.7 cr of operating revenue.

544647.name: Nephrocare Health Services Ltd (NephroPlus)
544647.summary: NephroPlus runs about 570 dialysis clinics in India, the Philippines, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Nepal and Saudi Arabia, charging a fee every time a kidney patient is dialysed – typically three sessions a week, for life. In India most clinics sit inside private hospitals or government hospitals, which supply the space while NephroPlus brings the machines, staff and consumables; the bill is paid by patients, insurers, government health schemes or, in PPP clinics, the state itself. Abroad, it earns three to five times more per session than in India.

payers.pays: A per-session dialysis fee; NephroPlus shares revenue with the host hospital (≈37% of revenue, H1 FY26 per RHP)

payers.who: Governments under PPP contracts (Indian states, Uzbekistan)
payers.pays: A fixed fee per treatment for free dialysis given to public-hospital patients (≈31%, H1 FY26 per RHP)

payers.who: Patients and national payers at standalone, acquired and home-dialysis services (e.g., PhilHealth in the Philippines)
payers.pays: Per-session fee, often at a tariff set by the national payer (residual ≈32%, derived from the RHP split)

Dialyzers, tubing, fluids and drugs per session (procurement scale cut COGS by 175 bps of revenue in Q1 FY27)
Revenue share for space and utilities under 7–15-year agreements (rate not disclosed)
Capex of ₹165 cr in FY26 (₹102 cr in H1 FY27) for new clinics and Philippine roll-ups

streams.name: India dialysis
streams.how: About 500 clinics in 314 cities, ~80% in tier-2/3 towns. Charged per session at about $22–23 (≈₹1,900–2,000) – captive clinics bill patients or schemes, PPP clinics bill the state at the tender rate.

streams.name: International dialysis
streams.how: Philippines (55+ clinics, about $111 a session, mostly paid by PhilHealth), Uzbekistan (a large PPP with the state, about $60), Kazakhstan (entered Q2 FY27, ~$75–80) and a Saudi JV. Rose to ~47% of revenue in H1 FY27.

mechanics: A patient with kidney failure needs dialysis about three times a week for the rest of their life (or until a transplant), so each patient is a recurring revenue stream: roughly 150 sessions a year. NephroPlus served 38,814 patients ('guests') at end-September 2026 and delivered 38.45 lakh treatments in FY26.

In India it uses three formats. Captive clinics (about 37% of group revenue in H1 FY26, per the RHP) sit inside 300+ private hospitals on a built-own-operate basis: the hospital gives space and utilities, NephroPlus funds machines and runs the unit, and the two share revenue. PPP clinics (about 31%, including Uzbekistan) are won by tender in public hospitals; the state pays a fixed fee per treatment, with roughly 3% annual escalation, and payments typically take three to four months. Standalone clinics are fewer and often acquired.

Prices are largely set by payers rather than by NephroPlus. In India the session price is about $22, and government rates change rarely but in big steps – CGHS raised its rate about 35% in October 2025 after over a decade. In the Philippines PhilHealth raised its standard rate by 55–60% in October 2024, and no further rise is expected for two to three years.

A clinic is a fixed-capacity box: each machine runs about three shifts a day, and the network runs at 74–75% utilisation (clinics above ~85% need spare slots for emergencies). Growth therefore comes mostly from adding clinics – about 80% of India growth – at 40–50 new clinics a year in India and 10–15 in the Philippines, plus a new country every 12–18 months.

The return per clinic differs sharply by market: capex per bed is ₹10–11 lakh in India with a 3.5–4 year payback, but ₹40–45 lakh in the Philippines with a 1–1.5 year payback because tariffs are five times higher. Greenfield clinics take 18–24 months to fill; acquired or captive clinics stabilise in 3–6 months.

Cash collection is the weak link: receivable days were 116 in FY26 (101 in Q1 FY27) because government and insurer payers pay slowly, and the company provides 2–2.5% of revenue for expected credit losses.

544647.costs: Each session carries variable costs – dialyzers, tubing, fluids and drugs – which scale with volume and fall as procurement scale grows (COGS ratio down 175 bps YoY in Q1 FY27). The fixed base per clinic is staff (technicians, nurses, doctors), the hospital revenue share in captive units, maintenance and depreciation of machines (≈8.7% of revenue). Capex is steady and growing (₹165 cr in FY26, expected higher in FY27) because capacity is only added clinic by clinic. Operating leverage comes from filling empty shifts in existing clinics and from mix: higher-tariff international clinics carry similar staff and consumable costs to India but earn three to five times the price, lifting adjusted EBITDA margin to 23.8% in FY26.
moat: Scale: about half of India's organised dialysis market and roughly 4.4x the next organised peer, giving purchasing power on consumables and machines.
Embedded hospital relationships: 300+ private hospitals on 7–15-year captive contracts, which competitors cannot easily displace mid-contract.
PPP track record and accreditations (31 JCI, 145 NABH centres) that win government tenders and foreign entries such as Uzbekistan and Saudi Arabia.
Sticky, recurring patients: dialysis patients rarely switch clinics, giving each clinic predictable volume once filled.

544802.name: Waterways Leisure Tourism Ltd
544802.summary: Waterways Leisure runs Cordelia Cruises, India's main domestic ocean cruise line: holidaymakers pay a cabin fare for 2-5 night sailings from Mumbai, Chennai and Kochi, and spend a little more on board. Almost all revenue (about 91%) is ticket sales, so the business behaves like an airline-hotel hybrid: one large fixed-cost asset whose profit swings with how full it sails and with fuel prices. It is now going from one ship to three, using leased ships.

payers.who: Retail holidaymakers, families and groups (about 62% booked direct, rest via travel agents)
payers.pays: Per-cabin fares for 2-5 night cruises, set dynamically by cabin type, date and itinerary, plus a fuel surcharge of USD 15-20 per person per day since 2026

payers.who: Guests on board, MICE clients and wedding parties
payers.pays: Onboard spend (specialty dining, bars, casino, spa, shore excursions), event and charter fees, and commissions

outflows.gets: Marine fuel: ₹1,480 per available passenger cruise day in FY26, jumping to ₹2,471 in Q2 FY27
Charter and lease payments (Empress is owned by Bay Cruise Investment Inc; Sky lease about USD 16m a year)

outflows.who: Outsourced hotel, crewing and entertainment contractors
outflows.gets: Food and beverage, housekeeping, crew wages (up ~16%) and shows
Port charges (with GST on domestic ports) and agent commissions on ~38% of cabins

streams.name: Cruise ticket sales
streams.how: Guests pay upfront for a cabin on a specific sailing; price depends on cabin category (interior to suite), season and itinerary, with dynamic pricing. Fares include main meals and standard entertainment.
streams.driver: Berths available × occupancy × average ticket price

streams.name: Onboard spend, events and other
streams.how: Extra spend once aboard (specialty restaurants, drinks, casino, spa, excursions) plus weddings, corporate MICE charters and commissions.
streams.driver: Guests × onboard spend per guest; number of wedding and charter dates

mechanics: Cordelia sells capacity measured in available passenger cruise days (APCD): beds × days at sea. In FY26 it had 566,752 APCD on one ship, the MV Empress (796 cabins, 2,005 beds), and sold 481,660 of them, an occupancy of 85%. Occupancy above 100% happens when third and fourth berths in cabins are filled by families.

Guests book on the website, app, a 148-person call centre or through travel agents. About 62% of cabins were sold direct in FY26, saving agent commission. Fares are paid upfront, often weeks or months before sailing, so the company holds customer advances (about ₹65 cr of bookings at the Q1 FY27 call) that fund working capital.

The average ticket price was about ₹10,980 per passenger in FY26 and total revenue per passenger about ₹12,000, so onboard spend is a thin layer on top. Management says ticket prices do not move much; growth comes from cabin mix. That is why the new ships matter: Sky has about 260 suites versus about 69 on Empress, and management expects per-guest revenue roughly 100% higher on Sky and 150% higher on Sun.

Costs per sailing are mostly fixed: the ship, crew, fuel to sail the route, port fees and the shore-side marketing team cost much the same whether the ship is 70% or 100% full. So each extra guest above breakeven drops largely to profit, which is why Q2 FY27 (monsoon, load factor 75.5%) and Q3-Q4 (Diwali, Christmas, wedding season) look so different.

Fleet growth is via time charters and leases rather than buying ships outright. The IPO raised ₹585 cr, of which ₹480 cr goes to deposits, advance lease rentals and monthly lease payments to a GIFT City (IFSC) leasing subsidiary. Cordelia Sky (1,002 staterooms) started sailing on 23 Oct 2026 and Sun follows about 11 months later; shore costs will then be shared across three ships.

544802.costs: This is a high fixed-cost model. Ship lease/charter, crew, hotel operations (outsourced F&B, housekeeping, entertainment), shore marketing and most of the fuel bill are committed once a schedule is published, so EBITDA swings sharply with occupancy and fuel: FY25 EBITDA margin was 36% at 92% occupancy, FY26 fell to 20% at 85%. Fuel is the most volatile line; VLSFO went from about USD 580/tonne to a USD 1,228 peak in 2026, and surcharges only apply to new bookings. Leasing keeps capex low but adds long-term dollar-linked obligations. Operating leverage comes from filling more berths and from spreading shore overheads across three ships.
moat: First mover and dominant player: about 79% share of India's domestic ocean cruise segment, with 7.3 lakh guests carried by March 2026.
Product tuned to Indian guests (Indian dining, Bollywood-themed shows, short 3-5 night trips for an average guest age of 34, onboard weddings) that foreign lines rarely match on Indian itineraries.
Direct distribution: about 62% of cabins sold direct, lowering commission and building a repeat database (loyalty programme 'Chairman's Club').
Itinerary access such as Lakshadweep islands and coastal ports that need local permissions and relationships.

544865.name: LEAP India Ltd
544865.summary: LEAP India rents out shared ('pooled') wooden pallets, plastic crates and forklifts to over 1,000 manufacturers and logistics firms, and charges them by the day or by the trip instead of selling the equipment. It buys the assets once (a pallet costs about ₹1,750), then rents each one for about ₹1.54 a day, collecting, repairing and reissuing it again and again over many years. It is India's largest pallet pool, with about 90% of the market by fleet size, so most of the money goes into owning a large fleet up front, which then earns roughly 50% EBITDA margins.

payers.pays: Daily hire per pallet or crate held, plus per-trip movement fees

payers.who: Automotive OEMs and parts makers (e.g. Daimler, Autoliv)
payers.pays: Daily hire for custom returnable crates and foldable containers

payers.who: Durables, 3PL, quick-commerce, textiles and others
payers.pays: Pallet/crate hire and forklift (MHE) rental via TARON

outflows.gets: Pooling capex, ~₹450 cr guided for FY27

outflows.gets: ₹156 cr in FY26 (₹128 cr staff + ₹28 cr contract labour)
Freight ₹77 cr and repairs ₹40 cr in FY26 to collect, fix and reposition assets
Interest ₹94 cr in FY26; cut sharply after ₹360 cr IPO-funded repayment

streams.name: Pallet pooling
streams.how: Customers pay a daily rent per pallet while it sits in their system (static hire), or a per-movement fee when a pallet travels one way from a maker to a distributor and LEAP collects it (movement/transfer hire).
streams.driver: Pallets on hire × utilisation × ₹/day yield

streams.name: Containers and crates
streams.how: Mainly automotive: foldable large containers and customised crates rented by the day on multi-year contracts; CHEP India (acquired Jan 2025) added much of this.
streams.driver: Crates deployed × utilisation (73.7% Q2 FY27)

streams.name: Forklift and MHE rental (TARON)
streams.how: Monthly rental of forklifts, many lithium-ion, often with LEAP's own operators supplied.
streams.driver: Machines deployed × monthly rental; ~82% utilisation

streams.name: Asset sales
streams.how: Outright sale of pallets, containers and inserts to customers who prefer to own.
streams.driver: One-off orders

streams.name: Scrap and other operating income
streams.how: Sale of scrap from damaged assets and provisions written back.
streams.driver: Fleet size and repair cycle

mechanics: LEAP buys standard pallets, crates and forklifts and keeps them in 27 fulfilment centres across India. A customer (say a beverage bottler) orders pallets; LEAP delivers them from the nearest depot and from that day charges rent for each pallet held. India's pallet pooling is still small: pooled pallets are about 9% of all pallets in India against roughly 90% in North America and the EU.

There are two ways to pay. In static hire the customer keeps pallets inside its own plant or warehouse and pays a daily rate. In movement hire the pallet travels loaded from the customer to its distributor, LEAP picks it up at the other end, and the customer pays per movement; LEAP handled about 2.8 million movements last year and targets 3.6–3.7 million in FY27.

Prices sit in 3–5 year contracts with built-in annual increases of about 5–6%, linked to a German wood price index so timber inflation is passed on. Average yield was ₹1.54 per pallet per day in Q1–Q2 FY27 against ₹1.45 a year earlier, which management puts at about ₹560 a year per pallet.

When a pallet comes back LEAP inspects, repairs and reissues it (1.4 million pallets were repaired in Q1 FY27), so one pallet bought for about ₹1,750 earns rent for many years. The economics turn on utilisation: the share of the fleet out on hire was 89.3% in Q2 FY27, against a 90–91% target, and every idle pallet still costs depreciation.

Customers are invoiced monthly on credit. Collection is slow: receivable days (DSO) were 122 in Q2 FY27, with a target below 90 by March 2027. Growth needs fresh capex every year, about ₹450 cr in FY27, so cash profit is reinvested in the fleet rather than paid out.

Operating costs are smaller and partly fixed: staff and contract labour ₹156 cr, freight ₹77 cr and repairs ₹40 cr in FY26. The lower-margin forklift business (about 30% EBITDA margin) dilutes the group margin as it grows.
moat: Network density: about 90% of India's pooling market by fleet, 27 depots and 10,100+ customer touchpoints mean pallets can be collected anywhere, which a new entrant cannot offer early on.
Pooling markets tend toward one or two players per country; LEAP absorbed CHEP India (the local arm of the global pooling leader) in January 2025.

Scale in sourcing (Plinova timber, Vimprotech plastics) and in repair lowers cost per pallet.

544866.name: Molbio Diagnostics Ltd
544866.summary: Molbio sells Truenat, a battery-run portable PCR machine that tests a sample for TB and other diseases in about an hour, and then sells the single-use test chips that only work on its own machines. Governments are the main buyers: India's central and state TB programmes paid about 80% of FY26 revenue under tendered rate contracts, mostly for kits. It is a 'razor and blade' model in which about 12,500 installed machines keep consuming roughly ₹590 kits.

payers.pays: Kits and devices at two-year tendered rate-contract prices

payers.who: State governments
payers.pays: Kits and devices bought under state orders off the rate contract

payers.pays: Devices, kits, X-ray systems at negotiated/distributor prices

₹87 cr in FY26, ≈6% of revenue

outflows.gets: Largely fixed costs
EBITDA loss ₹15 cr in H1 FY27

streams.name: Truenat test kits (chips)
streams.how: Each test uses a disposable chip and reagents sold per kit; government prices are set in tendered rate contracts, private and export prices are negotiated. TB is about 96% of kits sold.
streams.driver: Installed machines × tests run per machine × price per kit

streams.name: Truenat devices
streams.how: Sale of Trueprep sample-prep and Truelab analyser units (Uno, Duo, Quattro variants) under the same tenders and to private labs; each placement locks in future kit demand.
streams.driver: 2,200–2,600 devices a year

streams.name: Others (Prognosys X-ray, OptraSCAN, other)
streams.how: Digital and portable X-ray systems from 70%-owned Prognosys (FY26 revenue ₹154 cr) and digital pathology scanners from 60%-owned OptraSCAN.
streams.driver: Equipment orders, mostly public-health TB screening

mechanics: India's National TB Elimination Programme buys Truenat machines and places them in district and block-level centres; about 8,000–9,000 of an estimated 25,000–30,000 TB testing centres use Truenat. The machine runs on a battery, needs no air-conditioned lab, and reports TB and drug resistance in about an hour, which made it practical for small clinics.

Once a machine is installed, every test needs a Molbio chip-based kit; the system is closed, so no other kit works. That is why kits are about three-quarters of revenue and grow faster than device sales. Revenue per kit was about ₹590 in FY26 (₹628 in FY24), with raw material of about ₹325 per kit.

Pricing is not set by MRP but in tenders: the central government signs a two-year TB rate contract (renewed in 2026 at similar realisations), and states order against it. A one-month delay in that renewal pushed about ₹100 cr of H1 FY27 sales into H2, showing how lumpy the timing can be.
Delivery happens within weeks of an order, and governments typically pay 60–75 days after invoice; trailing receivable days were 77 in September 2026. H1 is usually 35–45% of the year's revenue.

Outside India, Truenat is one of two WHO-endorsed rapid molecular TB tests for initial diagnosis, so donor-funded programmes in Africa and Asia can buy it; exports were 10% of FY26 revenue and depend on Global Fund buying cycles. Newer assays (hepatitis, HPV, veterinary) and three new platforms aim to sell more kits per installed machine.

544866.costs: Materials are the largest cost at about 39% of FY26 revenue, and about 42% of inputs are imported, so currency and duty changes matter. Employees, the R&D subsidiary (about 6% of revenue) and plant overheads are largely fixed. Kit plants ran at about 58% and device lines at about 42% of capacity in FY26, and ₹72 cr of IPO money is going into automation that management says can support roughly 3x today's revenue with little extra capex; that is the source of operating leverage. Inventory is heavy (230 trailing days in June 2026) because government orders arrive in bursts. EBITDA margin fell from 28% in FY24 to 22% in FY26 as lower-margin subsidiaries and R&D grew; FY27 is guided at 24–25%.
moat: Closed system: every installed Truenat machine can only use Molbio kits, so the installed base produces recurring revenue.
Regulatory barriers: ICMR validation took about 13 years of R&D, and WHO endorsement for initial TB diagnosis is held by only two rapid molecular tests.
Incumbency in India's TB programme: management cites about 90% share of India's molecular diagnostics market, embedded in national testing guidelines and rate contracts.
Portable, battery-run design built for small clinics, where lab-based rivals need more infrastructure.

544915.name: Rentomojo Ltd
544915.summary: Rentomojo buys furniture and appliances (sofas, beds, fridges, ACs, water purifiers) and rents them to urban renters for a monthly fee that includes delivery, installation, repairs and relocation. When a subscription ends it collects, refurbishes and rents the same item out again, so one item can earn several times its cost over about 10 years. It is a capital-heavy lending-like business disguised as e-commerce: the edge is buying cheap, keeping items rented and making them last.

mechanics: A customer picks items on the app, website or one of 82+ experience stores, chooses a tenure and pays rent monthly; contracts auto-renew and can be cancelled early with a fee. Rentomojo delivers and installs, repairs or swaps faulty items, and moves the items if the customer relocates within a served city. The average subscription lasts about 18 months and about half of orders come from repeat customers.

Each item is a small financed asset. Rentomojo pays upfront (implied average value about ₹11,700 per item in Q2 FY27) and earns roughly ₹6,250 a year in rent per item (FY26), so gross rent covers cost in about two years (est.). Management estimates a 10-year useful life, and its FY2017 cohort has earned 5.1x its cost with 56% of items still on rent.

Returned items go to warehouses for refurbishment (over 6 lakh refurbishments in FY26 at about ₹19 cr) and back into the pool. Occupancy, the share of the fleet on rent, is the key lever: 83.3% in FY26 and 85.9% in Q2 FY27. Idle stock still depreciates.

Because customers pay monthly and Rentomojo pays suppliers upfront, growth consumes cash: operating cash flow is about 110% of EBITDA, but capex has run ahead, leaving free cash flow near zero in FY26. Contracted revenue not yet recognised was ₹293 cr at March 2026, giving visibility.

Pricing power is modest: average revenue per item rose about 4.6% YoY in Q2 FY27, mostly from mix (more ACs and sofas). Growth instead comes from more subscribers (+42.5% YoY), more items per subscriber (2.8) and new stores and cities, while 89.5% of FY26 revenue still came from the top 10 cities.

Cash operating costs were 47% of revenue in FY26: employees (₹61 cr), contract manpower (₹38 cr), logistics (₹28 cr), performance marketing (₹21 cr), refurbishment (₹19 cr) and IT (₹11 cr). Many of these scale with items handled, but warehouses, stores, tech and management are semi-fixed, so higher occupancy and longer asset life give operating leverage. Debt (net debt/equity ~0.28x) funds part of the fleet.
moat: Scale in a near-duopoly: about 42-47% of organised furniture and appliance rental revenue and 50-55% of live subscribers (with Furlenco the main rival).
Re-commerce know-how: data on item life, damage and refurbishment lets it keep 10-year-old assets earning, which a new entrant cannot price in.
Credit and collections data on 2.5 lakh+ subscribers, reducing default losses on unsecured monthly payments.
Dense warehouse and service network in core cities lowers delivery and pickup cost per item.

544937.name: National Stock Exchange of India Ltd
544937.summary: NSE earns most of its money as a toll on trading: brokers pay it a fee per ₹1 lakh traded in shares and futures, or per ₹1 lakh of premium in options, and pass it on to clients. Equity options alone, above all Nifty weekly-expiry contracts, supply about three-quarters of transaction charges, so a large share of a ₹16,600 cr revenue base rests on one retail-heavy product that SEBI closely regulates.

mechanics: A client trades through a broker; the order is matched on NSE and cleared by NSE Clearing, which stands between buyer and seller and collects margins. The broker pays NSE's transaction charge (shown on the contract note) and recovers it from the client, so NSE carries no credit risk and is paid within days.

Since SEBI's 'true-to-label' rule of 1 Oct 2024, NSE charges one flat rate to every broker instead of volume discounts. FY26 transaction charges reconcile closely with rate × volume: options ADT of ₹57,662 cr premium over ~250 days at ₹35.03 per lakh per side gives ≈₹10,100 cr (est.) against ₹9,998 cr reported.

Equity options dominate because premium volumes are huge and the rate per lakh is high. Weekly Nifty expiry alone generated ₹1,699 cr in Q2 FY27, 38% of total income. SEBI's late-2024 F&O measures (one weekly expiry per exchange, bigger lot sizes) cut FY26 options charges 1.9% and futures 14%, which is why FY26 transaction charges fell 4.2%.

The data and co-location business sells proximity and information: algorithmic firms pay for racks within NSE's data centre to shave microseconds and for direct feeds; this revenue grows with algo activity and is less volatile than trading fees.

Most cost is fixed (technology, people), so margins expand with volume: Q4 FY26 operating EBITDA margin was 73% versus 67% for FY26, which was depressed by SEBI settlement provisions. The clearing arm also holds large margin and fund balances, adding investment income, and corporate treasury stood at ₹34,699 cr in Sep 2026.

544937.costs: FY26 consolidated expenses were ₹6,127 cr, inflated by ₹1,432 cr of SEBI settlement fees; excluding that, costs run roughly a quarter of operating revenue. The main lines are technology (≈8.7% of operating revenue and growing mid-teens), employees (+18% YoY in Q2 FY27 due partly to the wage code), SEBI regulatory fees, clearing and settlement costs, contributions to the Core SGF, and CSR. Capex is guided at roughly ₹940 cr for FY27 (H1 ₹490 cr, H2 ~₹450 cr). Since revenue swings with volume while costs barely move, the operating margin ranges from mid-60s to mid-70s %.
moat: Liquidity network effect: ~92% of cash, 99.8% of equity futures and ~68–70% of options premium; a trader gets the best price where everyone else trades.
Index intellectual property: Nifty 50 and Bank Nifty are owned by NSE Indices, so rivals cannot list Nifty derivatives, and ETFs pay licence fees to track them.
Vertical integration: owning the clearing corporation, data business, co-location and index arm lets NSE capture fees at every step of a trade.
Regulatory and technology barriers: few exchange licences exist, and matching billions of orders a day with low latency took decades to build.

risks: SEBI F&O policy: further curbs on weekly expiries, lot sizes or retail eligibility hit the options line that supplies ~60% of operating revenue.
Concentration: Nifty weekly expiry alone is 38% of total income.
Competition: BSE's Sensex options have taken share; NSE's options premium share was ~68% in Q2 FY27 versus ~73% shown in its Q4 FY26 presentation.
Tax changes: higher STT or other taxes on derivatives (cited for the 11.7% fall in futures ADT) reduce volumes.
Regulatory/legal: past co-location and governance cases led to large settlements (₹1,432 cr in FY26); outages invite penalties.
